Discussion Summary of main results This review aimed to assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of infections in adults with solid tumours. Altogether, we identified 10 studies for inclusion in this review. Most studies included adults with malignant solid tumours of different types. Of these, three RCTs (3054 participants) evaluated vaccines to prevent herpes zoster, five studies (one RCT and four controlled NRSIs; 76,372 participants) evaluated vaccines to prevent influenza, and one RCT (2256 participants) evaluated vaccines to prevent COVID‐19. The RCTs assessing herpes zoster and COVID‐19 vaccines were funded by the manufacturers of the vaccines. We assessed the RCTs as being at low or moderate risk of bias, while we judged most of the controlled NRSIs to be at critical risk of bias, primarily due to concerns about confounding. Further, we identified two ongoing studies: one RCT evaluating the influenza vaccine and one controlled NRSI evaluating COVID‐19 vaccines. We also identified one completed but not yet published study, and 11 studies await classification due to unknown recruitment status, unclear randomisation, unclear control group, no outcomes of interest, results for participants with solid tumours were not reported separately, or unclear follow‐up after full vaccination. We did not identify RCTs or controlled NRSIs on vaccines for the prevention of pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, or diphtheria compared to placebo or no vaccine. In the following, only the results from RCTs are presented. Results from controlled NRSIs are detailed in the Effects of interventions section of the main text. Effects of interventions Vaccines for the prevention of herpes zoster compared to placebo or no vaccine See Table 1 . Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster decrease the incidence of herpes zoster up to 29.4 months after the final dose (high‐certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster probably make little or no difference in all‐cause mortality up to 28 days after the final dose (moderate‐certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster make little or no difference in adverse events (any grade) up to 30 days after the final dose (high‐certainty evidence) and probably make little or no difference in serious adverse events up to 30 days (moderate certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster increase the number of participants with localised events at the injection site up to 30 days after the final dose (high‐certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent herpes zoster may have little or no difference in the number of participants with systemic events up to 30 days after the final dose (low‐certainty evidence). Vaccines for the prevention of influenza compared to placebo or no vaccine See Table 2 . We are uncertain of the effects of vaccines on preventing influenza administered prior to surgery on all‐cause mortality up to 15 days post‐surgery (very low‐certainty evidence). We are uncertain of the effects of vaccines on preventing influenza in adverse events (any grade) up to 15 days post‐surgery (very low‐certainty evidence). We are uncertain of the effects of vaccines on preventing influenza administered prior to surgery on serious adverse events up to 15 days post‐surgery (very low‐certainty evidence). Vaccines for the prevention of COVID‐19 compared to placebo or no vaccine See Table 3 . Vaccines to prevent COVID‐19 probably decrease the incidence of COVID‐19 in participants without previous COVID‐19 infection up to six months after the second dose (moderate‐certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent COVID‐19 probably increase the number of participants with adverse events (any grade) up to 6 months after the second dose (moderate‐certainty evidence). Vaccines to prevent COVID‐19 may make little or no difference in the number of participants with serious adverse events up to 6 months after the second dose (low‐certainty evidence). Overall completeness and applicability of evidence The evidence summarised in this systematic review applies to vaccines for the prevention of herpes zoster, influenza, and COVID‐19 in adults with solid tumours. The findings are particularly relevant for healthcare providers involved in the care of these people, as they can guide vaccination strategies aimed at reducing infection risk. Understanding vaccine efficacy and safety is crucial for adults with solid tumours when making informed health decisions. The review indicates that certain vaccines, specifically those for herpes zoster and COVID‐19, demonstrate high‐ or moderate‐certainty evidence for reducing infection incidence. However, these vaccines may be associated with localised events at the injection site or any‐grade adverse events. It is important to note that the applicability of these findings may vary based on specific types of malignancy and their stages. Additionally, cancer therapies can significantly impact immune function and vaccine efficacy. However, due to insufficient data, we could not determine whether there are differences in outcomes between various malignancies or cancer therapies. The RCTs on herpes zoster included adults with diverse solid tumour types, such as breast cancer, colorectal cancer, and lung cancer ( Mullane 2013 ; Mullane 2019 ; Vink 2019 ), all receiving chemotherapy. This diversity allows for some comparison regarding how chemotherapy impacts vaccine efficacy across different cancers. Additionally, there are variations in vaccine types used in these studies. In Mullane 2013 , participants received a heat‐treated zoster vaccine, while Mullane 2019 administered an inactivated varicella‐zoster virus vaccine. In contrast, Vink 2019 employed an adjuvant recombinant zoster vaccine. A distinction in vaccine types may be important because different formulations can elicit varying immune responses, which may impact their effectiveness. In contrast to the herpes zoster vaccines, the RCT on influenza vaccines focused on adults with neck and oesophageal cancers undergoing surgery ( Goldmann 2015 ). This may limit the generalisability of the findings to other cancer types or treatment modalities, since participants were vaccinated prior to surgery. While there is very low certainty in the evidence on the effectiveness and safety of influenza vaccination for this particular subset of patients, it may not directly apply to those receiving immunotherapy or other surgical interventions. To supplement our findings from Goldmann 2015 , which was published as correspondence, we incorporated data from controlled NRSIs. For instance, INVIDIa‐2 and Amdisen 2024 reported on the incidence of influenza across a wider range of cancers, including participants undergoing immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy or chemotherapy. However, the studies primarily focused on severe disease and may not capture milder cases or asymptomatic infections, which are also important for assessing vaccine efficacy. In contrast, the data from controlled NRSI suggests that there is an effect on all‐cause mortality (moderate‐certainty) ( Gögenur 2021 ). This difference may arise from the different populations and the timing of the vaccination analysed in the included studies. Gögenur 2021 focuses on post‐surgery vaccination across multiple cancer types scheduled for surgery. The timing of the vaccination was within 30 days post‐surgery. The study measured all‐cause mortality as an outcome 180 days to three years post‐surgery. Nevertheless, this long‐term follow‐up provides insights into the potential impact of post‐surgery influenza vaccination on survival outcomes, thereby enhancing the completeness of results. However, while this study increases applicability by addressing diverse patient populations, it is essential to consider that factors influencing mortality may be multifactorial and not solely attributable to vaccination status. With respect to any‐grade adverse events, there remains uncertainty regarding the effects of influenza vaccines as indicated by both RCT ( Goldmann 2015 ) and controlled NRSI ( Wijn 2018 ) data. Wijn 2018 focused on adults with lung cancer receiving nivolumab. The study provides insights into the interactions between seasonal influenza vaccination and immunotherapy, but their targeted nature may restrict generalisability to other cancer treatments or patient populations not undergoing similar therapies. Influenza viruses are constantly evolving, and new strains can emerge. Influenza vaccines are adjusted annually to ensure better efficacy against the currently circulating strains ( WHO 2024 ). Therefore, it is important to interpret our findings on influenza vaccines with caution, as the included studies cover various influenza seasons. For example, the study by INVIDIa‐2 focuses on the 2019/2020 influenza season, while Wijn 2018 investigates the 2015/2016 and 2016/2017 seasons and Amdisen 2024 covers the seasons 2007/2008 to 2017/2018. Gögenur 2021 recruited participants between 2010 and 2015, and Goldmann 2015 covers the period from 2005 to 2008. This variability means that studies conducted across different seasons may yield results that are not directly comparable or applicable to current strains circulating within specific populations. In terms of COVID‐19 vaccines, Thomas 2022 focused on adults with various solid tumours, including breast cancer, prostate cancer, and melanoma, but did not provide clear information about specific cancer treatments received by the participants. We used data from a mixed population of solid tumours and haematological malignancies for adverse events and serious adverse events analyses since we expect similar events across both groups ( Copeland 2024 ; Javadinia 2022 ). Based on the RCT data, COVID‐19 vaccines probably decrease the incidence of COVID‐19 (moderate‐certainty). As the data only originates from a post‐hoc subgroup analysis, we supplemented our findings with data from controlled NRSIs. In contrast, controlled NRSI data presents uncertainty regarding their effects. The controlled NRSI by Zhao 2024 , specifically examined adults with hepatocellular carcinoma, a group facing unique immunological challenges due to liver dysfunction and underlying viral infections (e.g. hepatitis), which could influence vaccine efficacy differently than in other solid tumours ( Sachdeva 2015 ). Moreover, differences in vaccination regimens complicate comparisons. Thomas 2022 used the BNT162b2 vaccine, while Zhao 2024 , included multiple vaccines such as CoronaVac, BBIBP‐CorV, Zifivax, Convidecia, and BNT162b2. Notably, in Zhao 2024 , a small proportion of participants (6.5%) were not fully vaccinated. Such an incomplete vaccination status could lead to underestimating the potential protective effect of vaccination against infection. Furthermore, Thomas 2022 recruited participants between July 2020 to January 2021. Based on the recruitment period, we assume that participants may have been exposed to the SARS‐CoV‐2 variants alpha, beta and gamma. In contrast, Zhao 2024 recruited participants between January 2022 and October 2022 where omicron was prevalent. The evidence is only applicable to the SARS‐CoV‐2 variants prevalent at the time of the studies. It is also crucial for consumers and caregivers to be aware of the limitations regarding other vaccines due to insufficient data. Although there is a lack of evidence or only low to very low‐certainty evidence for many of the vaccines we were interested in for this particular group of adults with solid tumours, studies involving immunocompetent adults generally demonstrate that vaccines are well tolerated and effective in preventing severe outcomes and providing protection ( Demicheli 2018 ; Graña 2022 ; Plosker 2015 ). Due to the small number of included studies and lack of subgroup data in the primary studies, we were unable to adequately investigate the influence of effect modifiers, such as type of malignancy or treatment, through subgroup analyses. While most studies measure immunogenicity parameters such as antibody levels, seroconversion, or T‐cell responses, there are no correlates of protection defined. These surrogate endpoints are not considered as patient‐relevant outcomes. In this review, we focused only on patient‐relevant outcomes that we determined in a workshop conducted with people with cancer and their representatives. The involvement of adults with cancer and their representatives was essential to obtain a better understanding of patient‐important outcomes, to ensure a patient‐relevant focus for this systematic review, and to ensure that our findings remain relevant to consumers navigating complex healthcare decisions. Notably, none of the included studies measured quality of life. The studies included in our review were predominantly conducted in high‐income countries, which may not fully represent the challenges faced by low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs). According to Kamboj 2024 , the availability, accessibility, and utilisation of vaccines amongst adults with cancer in LMICs present significant hurdles. Limited resources and infrastructure, along with logistical barriers, often hinder vaccine distribution in these regions. Additionally, the high cost of vaccines can render them financially unattainable for many individuals. Consequently, the lack of access to vaccines leaves individuals with cancer in LMICs vulnerable to serious infections, which can adversely impact their health outcomes. Our review identified two ongoing studies, one RCT evaluating the influenza vaccine ( ACTRN12622000706774 ) and one controlled NRSI ( NCT05774171 ) evaluating COVID‐19 vaccines, which may provide further insights into vaccine efficacy once they are completed. One RCT evaluating an influenza vaccine has been completed, but no results have been published yet ( NCT02998736 ). We further categorised 12 studies with unknown recruitment status, unclear randomisation, unclear control group, no outcomes of interest or results for participants with solid tumours were not reported separately, or unclear follow‐up after full vaccination as 'awaiting classification' ( Bettinger 2022 ; EPIVAC ; Hayashi 2023 ; Kazemain 2023 ; Khaddour 2022 ; Klastersky 1986 ; Lau 2022 ; Leuva 2022 ; NCT01698177 ; NL‐OMON32477 ; Serrano 2022 ; Vinograd 2013 ). EPIVAC , a comprehensive population‐based cohort study, assessed the effectiveness of pneumococcal vaccines and provided data categorised for individuals with compromised immune systems. These encompass solid tumours, haematological malignancies, chronic severe nephropathy, asplenia, immunodeficiency (including HIV), and long‐term corticosteroid therapy or other immunosuppressive drugs. Since the data for these conditions were not analysed separately, we were unable to include the study. We will consider including these studies in an update of this review once results or sufficient information is available. Furthermore, we excluded numerous controlled NRSIs in which healthy individuals were used as a control group (e.g. Gomez 2021 ; Silveira 2019 ). Quality of the evidence Vaccines for the prevention of herpes zoster compared to placebo or no vaccine We included data from three RCTs to assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of herpes zoster compared to placebo or no vaccine. We rated the certainty of the evidence as high to low (see Table 1 ). We have high certainty in the evidence for the outcomes of incidence of herpes zoster, adverse events of any grade, and localised events at the injection site, and moderate certainty for the outcomes of all‐cause mortality and serious adverse events. Our main concern was imprecision due to wide confidence intervals. We have low certainty in the identified evidence for systemic events. We downgraded the certainty of the evidence for imprecision due to a wide confidence interval and inconsistency due to substantial statistical heterogeneity. Vaccines for the prevention of influenza compared to placebo or no vaccine We included data from one RCT and four controlled NRSIs to assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of influenza compared to placebo or no vaccine. We rated the certainty of the evidence as moderate to very low (see Table 2 ). For the RCT, we rated the certainty of the evidence as very low. Our main concerns were the risk of bias due to missing information on allocation concealment, missing data, selection of the reported results, and imprecision due to very wide confidence intervals, low number of participants, and low number of events (all‐cause mortality, adverse events of any grade, and serious adverse events). For controlled NRSIs, we rated the certainty of the evidence as moderate to very low. We downgraded the evidence for risk of bias due to confounding (incidence of influenza, all‐cause mortality, adverse events of any grade) and imprecision due to wide confidence intervals (incidence of influenza, adverse events of any grade). Vaccines for the prevention of COVID‐19 compared to placebo or no vaccine We included data from one RCT to assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of COVID‐19 compared to placebo or no vaccine. We rated the certainty of the evidence as moderate to low (see Table 3 ). Our main concerns were imprecision due to a low number of events or wide confidence intervals (incidence of COVID‐19, serious adverse events), or indirectness due to a mixed population including participants with solid tumours and haematological malignancies (any‐grade adverse events and serious adverse events). Potential biases in the review process We followed the guidelines of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions to minimise several potential biases in the review process ( Higgins 2024a ). An experienced information specialist (IM) developed the peer‐reviewed search strategy. The sensitive search included relevant electronic databases, as well as clinical trial registries, to ensure comprehensive coverage of available literature. To uphold the integrity and reliability of our review process, we conducted a comprehensive search for errata and retractions related to the studies included in our analysis. This step was essential for identifying potential biases arising from flawed or retracted research that could impact our conclusions. To supplement the lack of RCTs, we performed searches for controlled NRSIs when no RCTs were available for vaccines targeting specific infectious diseases. This also included vaccines to prevent influenza and COVID‐19, as the identified RCTs were published as correspondence ( Goldmann 2015 ) or reported data on solid tumour participants in a post hoc subgroup analysis ( Thomas 2022 ). While correspondence and post hoc analyses might provide valuable insights, they are generally considered less informative compared to primary research articles. Due to the limitations of these publication types, we decided to search for controlled NRSI as well. Given the differences in study design and potential biases associated with controlled NRSIs, we did not pool data from RCTs and controlled NRSIs. In addition, we made a conscious decision to categorise eligible studies that did not report any relevant outcomes as 'awaiting classification' rather than including or excluding them without having explored other ways to establish if our outcomes had been measured. This change reflects our commitment to ensuring that only studies with pertinent outcome data contribute to our findings. We included only studies with a minimum sample size of 20 participants per arm. This criterion was established to enhance the reliability and generalisability of our findings by ensuring that included studies had sufficient statistical power to detect meaningful effects. However, this inclusion criterion may also limit the number of available studies, potentially introducing bias if smaller but relevant studies are excluded from consideration (e.g. Chu 2013 ; Kumar 2012 ). In classifying interventions and outcomes, we based our decisions on the data available from the studies. We categorised the studies according to their design (RCTs versus controlled NRSIs) and focused on outcomes that were deemed important by adults with cancer and their representatives. Further, we distinguished between 'localised events at the injection site' and 'systemic events' as separate outcomes. Nonetheless, it is important to note that some studies reported symptoms such as headache or fever as single outcomes, which limited our ability to analyse these effects together ( Thomas 2022 ; Zhao 2024 ). In our analysis, we aimed to capture long‐term outcomes by using the longest available follow‐up data. However, this approach may present limitations, particularly due to variability in follow‐up durations across studies. Such differences may lead to inconsistencies in outcome reporting, introduce potential biases in assessing long‐term effects, and challenges in comparing results between studies with varying timeframes. In cases of missing data, if we needed more information, we contacted the study authors for additional data or relevant details. We received answers from the contact authors of three studies ( Amdisen 2024 ; Leuva 2022 ; Mullane 2013 ). However, we could not use the data from Leuva 2022 due to unclear follow‐up time after a full vaccination. The data from Amdisen 2024 were measured as incidence rates per 10,000 person‐years for the outcomes of incidence of influenza and all‐cause mortality. Due to the incompatible format of these outcomes, we only provide a narrative description, without assessing the risk of bias or certainty of the evidence. Given the small number of studies included in each comparison, the informative value of statistical methods for analysing publication bias, such as funnel plots, was limited. Moreover, due to the small number of included studies, we were unable to conduct any subgroup analyses that might have provided further insights into specific populations or intervention effects. Agreements and disagreements with other studies or reviews Notably, the ASCO guidelines addressed a research question similar to ours by systematically reviewing studies published between 2013 and 2023 ( Kamboj 2024 ). They focused on adults with solid tumours or haematological malignancies, including long‐term survivors and those who received haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, evaluating routine vaccines listed on the CDC immunisation schedules as well as travel vaccines. Their comparisons included placebo, different vaccines, or varying vaccination strategies. The outcomes assessed encompassed risk of infection, disease severity, mortality, immune responses, and vaccine safety ( Kamboj 2024 ). In terms of herpes zoster vaccines, Kamboj 2024 identified a study concerning solid tumours reporting adverse events ( Vink 2019 ), but did not include Mullane 2013 and Mullane 2019 as the guidelines focused on recombinant zoster vaccines (RZV). RZV, commonly known by its brand name Shingrix, is a recombinant form of glycoprotein E from the varicella‐zoster virus, which is a key protein involved in the virus's ability to infect cells ( Vink 2019 ). Our findings on herpes zoster vaccines align with those of a network meta‐analysis conducted by Xia 2022 , which reported that RZV demonstrated superior efficacy compared to placebo in immunocompromised individuals, achieving 60% efficacy (95% CI 49% to 69%). Adverse events associated with RZV were primarily related to injection site reactions and systemic effects, with no increased risk of serious adverse events or death. Kamboj 2024 indicated that "grade three solicited general adverse events" (i.e. moderate‐to‐severe adverse events actively monitored during the study), were reported by adults with cancer in both the vaccine and placebo arms but were more prevalent in the vaccine arms. This finding is consistent with our observations regarding the safety profile of herpes zoster vaccines. However, it is important to highlight that the analyses by Xia 2022 and Kamboj 2024 exclusively included studies assessing RZV, while our review encompassed studies assessing heat‐treated zoster vaccines ( Mullane 2013 ; Mullane 2019 ). Additionally, Xia 2022 and Kamboj 2024 included studies across various immunocompromised conditions such as haematological malignancies, renal transplantation, haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and HIV, alongside one study involving individuals with solid tumours ( Vink 2019 ), which was also part of our review. A previous Cochrane review on influenza vaccination conducted by Bitterman 2018 demonstrated that influenza vaccination is associated with reduced mortality and lower rates of infection‐related outcomes compared to non‐vaccination. This review encompassed a diverse population, including adults with solid tumours, haematological malignancies, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation. The inclusion of such a broad range of immunocompromised groups suggests that influenza vaccination may confer significant benefits across these populations. However, more recent systematic reviews have provided additional insights into the effects of influenza vaccination specifically in adults with cancer treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors. For instance, a systematic review by Tsiakos 2022 indicated that influenza vaccination appeared to have no effect on the mortality of adults with cancer receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors. Furthermore, it presented an acceptable safety profile, as it was not associated with an increased incidence of immune‐related adverse events, whether any grade or serious. In line with this, Lopez‐Olivo 2022 reported that vaccinated adults with cancer exhibited slightly lower rates of immune‐related adverse events compared to unvaccinated adults with cancer (32% versus 41%), reinforcing the notion that vaccination does not exacerbate safety concerns. Despite these findings, both reviews highlight the limitations in available data regarding other efficacy and safety outcomes. Tsiakos 2022 noted that limited data exist concerning progression‐free survival, humoral immunity response, cell‐mediated immunity response, and the incidence of influenza. Similarly, Lopez‐Olivo 2022 provided specific metrics indicating seroprotection rates for different influenza types (78% to 79% for type A and 75% for type B) but did not address these additional outcomes. However, most of the data are derived from observational retrospective studies with small sample sizes and unadjusted analyses ( Lopez‐Olivo 2022 ; Tsiakos 2022 ). The Cochrane review by Graña 2022 concluded that most COVID‐19 vaccines reduce or likely reduce the occurrence of confirmed symptomatic COVID‐19 when compared to placebo. For some vaccines, there is high‐certainty evidence supporting their effectiveness in reducing severe or critical disease. Our findings align with this conclusion, as we also observed a reduction in the incidence of COVID‐19 amongst vaccinated participants without previous infection (moderate‐certainty evidence). Kamboj 2024 further reported numerous studies examining immunologic parameters related to COVID‐19 vaccination amongst adults with cancer. They identified five controlled NRSIs demonstrating reduced rates of hospitalisation and mortality or decreased COVID‐19 sequelae in vaccinated versus unvaccinated adults with cancer. However, these studies did not exclusively focus on adults with solid tumours but also included adults with haematological malignancies ( Kamboj 2024 ). This broader inclusion may account for some variability in outcomes, but it underscores the importance of vaccination across different cancer types. In terms of vaccine safety, our observations regarding adverse events are consistent with those reported by Javadinia 2022 , who noted that COVID‐19 vaccination in adults with cancer is generally well‐tolerated regardless of cancer type. Both systemic and local adverse events, including fatigue, hypersensitivity reactions, fever, asthenia, vomiting, headaches, muscle and joint pain, chills, transient lymphadenopathy, and injection site reactions, were reported across various studies. While Javadinia 2022 highlighted that most vaccine‐related side effects were grade two at most, they also pointed out the challenges posed by differing assessment methods across studies, which complicate meta‐analysis efforts, such as the lack of reporting on the exact prevalence of PCR‐confirmed COVID‐19 infections and their outcomes. Additionally, many studies included in their review lacked a control group or used healthy controls, complicating the analysis still further ( Javadinia 2022 ). Our review reveals notable gaps in the literature concerning other vaccines. Kamboj 2024 reported an absence of eligible studies for hepatitis B, tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis vaccines. This lack of data aligns with our findings regarding the limited research available on certain vaccinations for adults with solid tumours. Furthermore, Kamboj 2024 identified only one RCT that examined the timing of pneumococcal vaccination. Authors' conclusions Implications for practice In adults with solid tumours, herpes zoster vaccines reduce the incidence of herpes zoster (high‐certainty evidence), although localised events at the injection site occur more frequently than with placebo or no vaccine (high‐certainty evidence). It is uncertain whether influenza vaccines affect all‐cause mortality, adverse events of any grade, or serious adverse events (very‐low certainty evidence); the incidence of influenza was not measured in the studies. Vaccines for preventing COVID‐19 probably decrease the incidence of COVID‐19 in adults without prior infection (moderate‐certainty evidence), but they probably increase adverse events of any grade (moderate‐certainty evidence). We found no randomised controlled trials or controlled non‐randomised studies of interventions that investigated the use of vaccines compared to placebo or no vaccine for the prevention of pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, or diphtheria, in adults with solid tumours. Implications for research We have identified two ongoing studies, one RCT evaluating an influenza vaccine ( ACTRN12622000706774 ) and one NRSI evaluating COVID‐19 vaccines ( NCT05774171 ). Additional research, preferably RCTs, is necessary to assess a wider range of available vaccines against infectious diseases such as pneumococcal disease, Haemophilus influenzae type b disease, meningococcal disease, pertussis, hepatitis B, tetanus, polio, or diphtheria, for which we did not identify any RCTs or prospective NRSIs. This lack of research limits our understanding of how these vaccines perform in adults with solid tumours. While we advocate conducting RCTs to obtain robust evidence, if such studies are not possible for ethical reasons, retrospective (matched) analyses of individuals with cancer who have or have not received the respective vaccination could provide some insights. Future studies should include individuals of various age groups and those with different types of solid tumours undergoing diverse treatments (such as chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and targeted therapy). This diversity is crucial, because different age groups may respond differently to vaccines due to variations in immune system function, and individuals with solid tumours may be undergoing treatments that affect their immune response. When investigating multiple malignancies, it is important to report results as subgroups. This approach allows researchers to identify specific populations that benefit most from vaccination and understand under which cancer therapies the vaccines may be less effective in preventing infection. Additionally, it needs to be investigated whether passive immunisation with monoclonal antibodies may offer more protection than vaccines for immunocompromised or immunosuppressed individuals. Research should not just focus on the usual immunological laboratory parameters, especially in populations where established correlates of protection are still lacking. The outcomes measured should be patient‐centred and important, such as the incidence of infection (tracking how often vaccinated individuals contract the targeted infectious disease), quality of life (assessing how vaccination impacts patients' overall well‐being and daily functioning), all‐cause mortality (evaluating whether vaccination correlates with mortality rates amongst individuals with solid tumours), and adverse events (monitoring any negative side effects resulting from vaccination). Additionally, studies should take into account periods when the risk of infection is heightened. For instance, during flu season (typically October to March), individuals with compromised immune systems may face increased risks. Future research should investigate potential effect modifiers that could influence the effectiveness of vaccines for preventing infectious diseases. These might include patient demographics (age, sex, comorbidities) and treatment modalities (type and timing of cancer therapies). Importantly, future research must also address the unique challenges faced by low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs), where barriers such as limited healthcare infrastructure, vaccine availability, and socioeconomic factors can significantly impact vaccination efforts. By understanding how these characteristics impact vaccine efficacy in LMIC contexts, alongside other factors influencing outcomes in high‐income settings, healthcare providers can tailor vaccination strategies to individual patient needs more effectively. In summary, addressing these gaps through rigorous research will enhance our understanding of vaccine effects across diverse patient populations. By prioritising patient‐centred outcomes and considering various factors influencing vaccine efficacy, including those specific to LMICs, we can optimise vaccination strategies to improve health outcomes for individuals at risk for infectious diseases. between protocol and review Differences between the published protocol ( Bora 2023 ) and this full review are as follows. Title We made minor edits to the title in order to use UK spelling ('tumours') and Cochrane style, i.e. 'for preventing' rather than 'for the prevention of'. Objectives We changed the wording from "To assess the benefits and harms of vaccines for the prevention of infections in adults with solid tumours" to "To assess the benefits and risks of vaccines for the prevention of infectious diseases in adults with solid tumours." Type of interventions We changed the wording to "We included vaccines for the prevention of the following infectious diseases in adults with solid tumours" and listed the diseases of the vaccines they protect against instead of the pathogens to specify the diseases targeted by these vaccines. Types of outcome measures Instead of including studies regardless of the reported outcome data, we decided to categorise eligible studies that did not report any of the relevant outcomes as 'awaiting classification'. We previously listed 'local events at the injection site' and 'systemic events' under the outcome 'adverse events of special interest'. As these were intended to represent two separate outcomes, we no longer summarise them under one bullet point in the review but list them separately. Selection of studies We used the Rayyan software ( Ouzzani 2016 ) instead of Covidence to screen the references. We listed excluded studies that initially appeared to meet the inclusion criteria, but that we later excluded, in the 'Characteristics of excluded studies' table, with the reasons for their exclusion, instead of listing all excluded studies. Search methods Although at least one RCT was identified for vaccines against influenza and COVID‐19, we searched for NRSIs, as the one RCT on influenza vaccines was published as correspondence only, and the one RCT on COVID‐19 reported on participants with solid tumours in a post hoc subgroup analysis. To ensure the integrity and reliability of the studies included in this review, we searched for errata or retractions related to the included studies that may have been published on MEDLINE, Embase, or Retraction Watch. We did not contact experts in the field to retrieve information on unpublished studies. If required, we contacted the authors for supplementary information. Assessment of reporting bias As we did not pool the data in the meta‐analysis and included fewer than 10 studies per comparison, we did not generate funnel plots to assess reporting bias. Subgroup analysis and investigation of heterogeneity We removed the planned subgroup analysis based on duration of follow‐up (e.g. shorter versus longer follow‐up) because we grouped the measurement time points of eligible outcomes into short‐term (up to 12 weeks after full vaccination), medium‐term (from 12 weeks to 6 months after full vaccination) and long‐term (more than 6 months after full vaccination) observations, if sufficient data was available (see Types of outcome measures ). Due to the limited number of studies that provided relevant data for our critical outcome, we did not perform meta‐analysis and thus conducted no subgroup analysis. If heterogeneity was above 75%, we planned to explore this with subgroup and sensitivity analysis. Despite considerable heterogeneity in Analysis 1.5 , we decided to keep the pooled effect estimate, as the effects of the individual studies were clearly on one side. We were unable to conduct the planned sensitivity analyses because the risk of bias for these RCTs was classified as either 'low' or 'some concerns'. Summary of findings and assessment of the certainty of the evidence We created the summary of findings tables manually and did not use GRADEpro GDT . We added a section on consumer involvement during protocol development. The order of the comparisons and summary of findings tables was prioritised by clinical experts, based on relevance to decision‐makers. If evidence from both RCTs and NRSIs was available for a single outcome, only the RCT data were presented in the summary of findings tables. documents.title: Lightweight versus heavyweight synthetic mesh for inguinal hernia repair.
documents.abstract: OBJECTIVES: This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review (intervention). The objectives are as follows: To assess the benefits and risks of lightweight mesh compared with heavyweight mesh in any open mesh-reinforced hernia repair as well as in laparoscopic repair (TAPP, TEP, or robotic TAPP) in adults with an inguinal hernia.

Objectives This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review (intervention). The objectives are as follows: To assess the benefits and risks of lightweight mesh compared with heavyweight mesh in any open mesh‐reinforced hernia repair as well as in laparoscopic repair (TAPP, TEP, or robotic TAPP) in adults with an inguinal hernia. status released display-pdf yes is-olf no is-manuscript no is-preprint no is-journal-matter no is-scanned no is-retracted no Collection date 2025. Background Description of the condition Inguinal hernias make up 75% of abdominal wall hernias, with lifetime risks of 27% for men and boys and 3% for women and girls ( Kingsnorth 2003 ). Indirect inguinal hernias (IIHs), occurring externally or laterally, surpass direct inguinal hernias (DIHs) at a ratio of roughly 2:1 ( Kingsnorth 2003 ). Indirect inguinal hernias arising from patent processus vaginalis may be due to cryptorchidism ( Favorito 2005 ), lack of carbachol response, absence of cholinergic receptors ( Tanyel 1999 ), absence of myofibroblasts ( Tanyel 2001 ), absence of apoptotic nuclei ( Tanyel 2002 ), failure of smooth muscle apoptosis, catecholaminergic activity related to luteinising and gonadotropin‐releasing hormones, and deficiencies involving epithelial‐mesenchymal transition ( Hori 2021 ; Momoh 1982 ; Somuncu 2020 ; Tanyel 1999 ; Tanyel 2001 ; Tanyel 2002 ; Tanyel 2004 ). Increased abdominal pressure (caused by obesity, constipation, and coughing) ( Holzheimer 2005 ), diabetes ( Holzheimer 2005 ), smoking ( Holzheimer 2005 ), collagen distribution ( Henriksen 2016 ; Koruth 2017 ), peritoneal dialysis ( Sodo 2016 ), radical prostatectomy ( Miyajima 2018 ), and family history ( Burcharth 2014 ) are potential risk factors for groin hernias ( HerniaSurge Group 2018 ). Inguinal hernia is usually asymptomatic but may present dull aching or dragging discomfort with a bulge in the groin, and the disappearance of the bulge in the supine position raises clinical suspicion of inguinal hernia ( Shakil 2020 ). Clinical evaluation remains a mainstay for diagnosis; the use of ultrasound, dynamic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)/computed tomography (CT) (with Valsalva), and herniography is recommended in selective situations with obscure inguinal pain or swelling, or both ( HerniaSurge Group 2018 ; Simons 2009 ). Indications for surgery include symptomatic and/or acutely irreducible inguinal hernia, with the option of watchful waiting for asymptomatic/minimally symptomatic inguinal hernia ( HerniaSurge Group 2018 ; Miserez 2014 ; Simons 2009 ; Stabilini 2023 ). Surgical challenges with or without increased risk of complications for inguinal hernia repair occur in elderly people ( Perez 2022 ), infants ( Ramchandran 2020 ), and people with comorbidities like liver cirrhosis ( Li 2020 ), diabetes ( Hellspong 2017 ), chronic renal failure ( Luk 2020 ; Sodo 2016 ), chronic smoking ( Yergin 2023 ), collagen disorders ( Fogel 2013 ), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease ( Dai 2019 ), and obesity ( Chinn 2022 ). The risk of untreated inguinal hernia (strangulation) along with complications of inguinal hernia surgery including acute or chronic pain and recurrence needs careful assessment for each person individually ( HerniaSurge Group 2018 ; Miserez 2014 ; Ramsay 2020 ; Simons 2009 ; Stabilini 2023 ). Inguinal hernia surgery is one of the most performed surgeries worldwide ( Kingsnorth 2003 ). The use of mesh in inguinal hernia repair was initially proposed in the 1960s for elderly people with hernia recurrence ( Lichtenstein 1989 ). Promising results from these cases led to the adoption of mesh in younger people with primary inguinal hernia ( Amid 2003 ). In comparison to non‐mesh or suture‐only repairs, with the benefits of low cost and usefulness in low‐resource settings, mesh repair has been found to reduce recurrence rates and neurovascular injury ( Lockhart 2018 ). The tension‐free mesh‐based repair of inguinal hernia has been the mainstay of treatment for several decades, as recurrence rates have been shown to be reduced by up to 50% ( Weyhe 2007 ). The standard of care practice in inguinal hernia repair in elective settings thus involves the use of prosthetic mesh ( Bisggard 2007 ; van Veen 2007 ). In general, in light of recent cases of pelvic mesh complications reported in the UK ( Dyer 2020 ), and the UK’s 2020 Cumberlege review criticism of regulatory failures and call for better oversight, informed consent, and support for affected patients ( Cumberlege 2020 ), complications related to mesh usage in other surgeries including inguinal hernia also deserve attention. The use of mesh in inguinal hernia repair, while effective in reducing recurrence rates, has been increasingly scrutinised due to its association with a range of postoperative complications. Common mesh‐related symptoms include chronic groin pain, foreign body sensation, and a feeling of heaviness or discomfort, which can persist long after the initial recovery period ( Pierides 2016 ; Wong 2018 ). Additionally, an impact on sexual function has been reported, including dysejaculation, reduced libido, and erectile discomfort, which may stem from nerve irritation or entrapment, mesh positioning, or scar tissue formation ( Aykanat 2022 ; Ece 2018 ). In a systematic review by Nienhuijs 2007 , the incidence of chronic pain was found to be 11%. This chronic pain is often neuropathic in nature, attributed to entrapment or injury of nerves such as the ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric, or genitofemoral nerves during or after the mesh placement. Given these findings, the choice of mesh type (e.g. lightweight versus heavyweight, absorbable versus permanent) and surgical technique (e.g. open versus laparoscopic) ( Haladu 2022 ) has become a focus of ongoing research and clinical debate. Subsequently, attention has now shifted towards chronic pain and quality of life outcomes apart from recurrence ( Heniford 2018 ; Renshaw 2022 ), with the use of certain modifications in mesh usage, such as the use of lightweight mesh (LWM) (< 50 g/m 2 ) in place of heavyweight mesh (HWM) (> 70 g/m 2 ), to address these complications ( Prakash 2016 ; Smietanski 2012 ). Moreover, another study concluded that while both meshes can cause cytomorphological changes in adjacent neural tissue through foreign body reaction and compression, the HWM is associated with more pronounced ilioinguinal nerve degeneration ( Keskinkılıç 2023 ). In a systematic review by Bakker 2021 , an increase in the risk of recurrence with the use of LWM as compared to HWM was found to be statistically significant, with overall recurrence rates ranging from 1% to 2%. One study concluded that LWM should be used in indirect, smaller hernia defects and HWM in direct and larger hernia (hernia > 3 cm) defects due to the increased risk of recurrence with LWM ( Melkemichel 2018 ). Other studies have reported comparable rates of infection ( Wu 2020 ), seroma ( Wu 2020 ), effect on sexual life, and male fertility ( Hu 2019 ) between LWM and HWM. Description of the intervention Inguinal hernia repair with mesh can be performed by various techniques, including open repairs like Lichtenstein repair, mesh plug repair, plug and patch, bilayer repair, preperitoneal repair, and laparoscopic techniques like transabdominal preperitoneal repair (TAPP), totally extraperitoneal repair (TEP), extended totally extraperitoneal repair (eTEP), robotic‐assisted laparoscopic repair, and single‐incision laparoscopic surgery hernia repair ( Prakash 2016 ; Smietanski 2012 ; Wong 2018 ). The use of LWM has been studied in both open and laparoscopic inguinal hernia surgery ( Sajid 2012 ; Sajid 2013 ). Among the various types of commercially available meshes, recommendations on the best type of mesh remain a matter of debate ( HerniaSurge Group 2018 ; Miserez 2014 ; Simons 2009 ; Stabilini 2023 ). While European Hernia Society guidelines advise (Grade B) using lightweight/material reduced mesh in open inguinal hernia repair with caution in large direct hernias ( Miserez 2014 ), other mechanical mesh properties such as weight, pore size, elasticity, porosity, and strength can affect postoperative outcomes ( Zhu 2015 ). However, mesh weight has been a widely studied parameter, and thus comparing LWM to HWM, using LWM < 50 g/m 2 and HWM > 70 g/m 2 as cut‐off points, assumes importance with the idea of the need to balance the risk of pain‐related complications with HWM and the risk of hernia recurrence with LWM ( HerniaSurge Group 2018 ). How the intervention might work Tissue strengthening by a strong mesh aponeurotic scar tissue complex has a bearing on overall efficacy of the repair, and thus the debate about higher strength of HWM versus decreased risk of contiguous tissue entrapment and chronic pain in LWM has gained prominence ( Keskinkılıç 2023 ; Prakash 2016 ; Smietanski 2012 ). Furthermore, the use of LWM in open inguinal hernia surgery has been found to surpass HWM with regard to chronic pain and foreign body sensation, but with no effect on recurrence rates ( Sajid 2012 ). Regarding laparo‐endoscopic repairs, the incidence of chronic groin pain is already less, and thus the relationship between decreased chronic groin pain and the use of LWM becomes difficult to determine ( Sajid 2013 ). Why it is important to do this review There are published Cochrane reviews comparing laparoscopic versus open surgery ( Gupta 2017 ) for inguinal hernia and mesh fixation versus no mesh fixation ( Lockhart 2018 ) in inguinal hernia. Regarding the weight of mesh in inguinal hernia, contradictory evidence exists, with a systemic review finding that the use of LWM in laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair did not offer a reduced risk of chronic pain or any change in the recurrence risk when compared with HWM ( Currie 2012 ). Another systemic review found a reduced incidence of chronic groin pain after laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair with LWM, with no effect on the risk of hernia recurrences ( Sajid 2013 ). This review will complement these studies by adding to the current evidence evaluating the type of mesh (lightweight or heavyweight) used in inguinal hernia surgery. Thus, this Cochrane review will encompass the use of heavy and lightweight meshes in inguinal hernia surgery by Lichtenstein repair and laparoscopic repair (TAPP, TEP, or robotic TAPP). Objectives To assess the benefits and risks of lightweight mesh compared with heavyweight mesh in any open mesh‐reinforced hernia repair as well as in laparoscopic repair (TAPP, TEP, or robotic TAPP) in adults with an inguinal hernia. Methods Criteria for considering studies for this review Types of studies We will include parallel‐arm randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing synthetic LWM versus synthetic HWM without restrictions on publication status or language. We will not include quasi‐RCTs (e.g. randomised on the basis of date of birth, participant's registration number, or the order in which participants were recruited) or cross‐over or cluster‐RCTs. We will include studies irrespective of their publication status, unless exclusion is explicitly justified. We will include unpublished data if shared by study authors and will perform a sensitivity analysis to check the effect of excluding such studies on the main analysis. Types of participants We will include all adult participants (aged 18 and over) with an inguinal hernia undergoing elective inguinal hernia repair with prosthetic mesh placement. We will include studies with a paediatric population (aged less than 18 years) if > 90% of participants are adults, even if the data on the adult population cannot be extracted separately. Types of interventions Types of inguinal hernia repair Open techniques will include any open synthetic mesh‐reinforced repair. Laparoscopic techniques will include: TAPP; TEP; robotic TAPP. We will consider open synthetic mesh‐reinforced repair (e.g. Lichtenstein repair) and laparo‐endoscopic technique for elective surgical repair of an uncomplicated inguinal hernia with the use of prosthetic mesh (lightweight and heavyweight). Types of synthetic mesh We will include lightweight mesh (non‐absorbable polypropylene; absorbable poliglecaprone or polyglactin) of < 50 g/m 2 and heavyweight mesh (non‐absorbable polypropylene) of > 70 g/m 2 as cut‐off points ( Currie 2012 ; Klinge 2012 ; Melkemichel 2018 ; Stabilini 2023 ; Zhu 2015 ). We will exclude studies reporting usage of mesh weight between 50 g/m 2 and 70 g/m 2 . We will exclude studies reporting the usage of mesh in an emergency setting or complicated hernia. Types of outcome measures We will include all studies fulfilling the study, participant, and intervention criteria irrespective of reported outcomes. If the following outcome measures are not reported in the studies, we will contact the study author or sponsor to provide the missing data. If we do not receive a response, we will send a follow‐up email two weeks later. The study will be included irrespective of response. Primary outcomes Chronic pain: pain persisting beyond three months postoperatively ( Merskey 1986 ). Visual analogue scale (VAS) will be the preferred measurement tool; we will consider a minimal clinical importance difference of 1 on a scale of 0 to 10. We will consider chronic pain on a VAS or other scales both as continuous outcome data and dichotomous data (pain/no pain), if reported as separate outcomes by the study investigators. Hernia recurrence: clinically or radiologically diagnosed; only trials reporting follow‐up of more than three months will be assessed ( Akolekar 2008 ; Post 2004 ) Secondary outcomes Surgical‐site infections (as defined by the included studies) within 30 days and within 90 days of repair. Mesh infection (clinico‐radiological) within 30 days and within 90 days of repair. Haematoma/seroma within 30 days and within 90 days of repair. Surgical complications, classified by the Clavien‐Dindo classification ( Dindo 2004 ), within 30 days of repair (Grade 1 to Grade 4). The outcome will be dichotomised into Grades 1 to 2 and Grades 3 to 4. We will report outcomes in the short term (≤ 90 days) and long term (> 90 days). Clinical recurrence or reoperation for recurrence within 30 days, within 90 days, and within one year of repair. Reoperation due to complications (e.g. infection, seroma, bleeding) within 30 days of repair and within 90 days of repair. Impact on sexual function and fertility data (testicular pain, dysejaculation) within 30 days and within 90 days of repair. Quality of Life (QoL) outcomes: disease‐specific QoL outcomes as advocated by recent updates of HerniaSurge guidelines ( Stabilini 2023 ); we will assess Hernia‐Related Quality of Life Survey (HerQLes) ( Renshaw 2022 ) and Carolinas Comfort Scale ( Heniford 2018 ) at one‐year postoperatively only as reported in the RCTs. We will consider a minimal clinical importance difference of 15.6 on a scale of 0 to 100 in HerQLes ( Renshaw 2022 ). Search methods for identification of studies Electronic searches We will search the following databases, without language or date restrictions: Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) to date of search; MEDLINE via PubMed (1946 to date of search); Embase (1974 to date of search). We will use the preliminary search strategies for MEDLINE to search the other databases for study reports, which we will modify as per database requirements. We will use methods and filters as mentioned in Lefebvre 2020 . The Ovid MEDLINE search strategy is presented in Appendix 1 . Searching other resources We will check the reference lists of all included studies and systematic reviews for primary studies. We will search the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform ( www.who.int/clinical-trials-registry-platform ) and US National Institutes of Health Ongoing Trials Register ClinicalTrials.gov (clinicaltrials.gov) for ongoing and completed trials. We will contact authors or sponsors for any information about missing data or possible publication of a relevant clinical trial. We will search for errata, expressions of concern, corrigenda, retractions, etc. from included studies on MEDLINE and Embase and report the date of this search in the review. Data collection and analysis Selection of studies We will import all search records into Covidence , which two review authors (AKP and BPS) will independently screen based on title and abstract for potential relevance. We will link multiple reports of a single study under a single reference ID. We will obtain the full‐text reports of those studies deemed potentially relevant and import these into Covidence . The same two review authors (AKP and BPS) will independently screen the full texts for inclusion in the review. Any discrepancies will be resolved in consultation with a third review author (AK). If uncertainty remains, we will contact the corresponding author or sponsor. In the case of potentially eligible studies for which a review author is an author, screening will be done by another review author to avoid any conflict. We will provide the reasons for exclusion of excluded studies in the 'Characteristics of excluded studies' table. We will present the study selection process in a PRISMA flow diagram ( Liberati 2009 ). Data extraction and management Use of a data extraction form The pilot data extraction form will be prepared and checked in Covidence . Two review authors (AKP and BPS) will independently perform data extraction in Covidence , and then consensus will be taken. We will contact the corresponding study author or sponsor for clarification or missing data as needed. A reminder will be sent after two weeks in the case of no response. The data extraction form will include the following information. Study identification: study ID, country, contact details of the corresponding author, clinical trial registration number, status of a clinical trial, and sponsor details. Method: study design and setting, aim, year of study, number of study centres, unit of allocation, follow‐up visits by participants, key conclusion of study. Participants: inclusion criteria, exclusion criteria, baseline group differences if any, gender, participants' clinical condition including size of hernia, diagnostic criteria used, total number randomised, number lost to follow‐up/withdrawn with reason. Interventions: type of intervention and comparison, details of intervention and comparison, any other procedure or concomitant medications, numbers of and reasons for participants moved from intended intervention. Outcomes: outcomes and their numerical values in the format that will be utilised in meta‐analysis. We will divide outcome reporting into short term if follow‐up is ≤ 90 days, and long term if follow‐up is > 90 days. We will note any conflicts of interest of study authors. We will record information needed to assess the risk of bias and the certainty of evidence as per GRADE recommendations using GRADEpro GDT . After consensus regarding the extracted data is agreed upon, one review author (AKP) will import data into RevMan 2025 , which another review author (BPS) will check for completeness. We will present details of the included studies in the 'Characteristics of included studies' table. We will present any data not included in meta‐analysis as a narrative synthesis. Assessment of risk of bias in included studies Two review authors (AKP and BPS) will independently assess risk of bias in the included studies using Cochrane's RoB 2 tool ( Sterne 2019 ). Any discrepancies will be resolved in consultation with a third review author (HSP). We will base our assessment on the following five domains. Bias arising from the randomisation process Bias due to deviations from the intended interventions Bias due to missing outcome data Bias in measurement of the outcome Bias in selection of the reported result We will quantify the effect of an assignment as 'intention‐to‐treat'. We will use different signalling questions of the RoB 2 tool to rate each domain as 'low risk of bias', 'some concerns', or 'high risk of bias'. The risk of bias judgement for all the domains will be summarised for each outcome across all included studies. We will report signalling questions that are available online using the Excel tool at www.riskofbias.info/welcome/rob-2-0-tool/current-version-of-rob-2 . We will present a risk of bias summary. The risk of bias assessment will inform the GRADE assessment of the certainty of evidence. We will conduct sensitivity analyses by removing studies judged to be at high risk of bias or with some concerns. We will assess risk of bias for the following outcomes: chronic pain, hernia recurrence, quality of life, surgical‐site infections, mesh infection, haematoma/seroma, surgical complications, clinical recurrence or reoperation for recurrence, reoperation due to complications (e.g. infection, seroma, bleeding), and fertility data. Measures of treatment effect We will perform analysis using RevMan 2025 . We will express dichotomous outcomes as risk ratio (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and continuous outcomes as mean difference (MD) or standardised mean difference (SMD) with 95% CIs. We will use SMD if the outcome is measured using different scales. The surgical complication as per classification by the Clavien‐Dindo (categorical outcome) will have more than two categories, and will be dichotomised into Grades 1 to 2 and Grades 3 to 4. We will report outcomes in the short term (≤ 90 days) and long‐term (> 90 days). If an outcome is reported at different times in a study, we will use data from the latest available time to short term or long term provided at least 30‐day follow‐up data are available. We will assess QoL outcomes (HerQLes and Carolinas Comfort Scale ( Heniford 2018 )) at one‐year postoperatively as reported in RCTs as a continuous outcome. Unit of analysis issues The unit of analysis for parallel‐group RCTs will be participants assigned to any type of intervention or comparison. For multi‐arm trials, we will use data from those intervention arms that will be included as per review inclusion criteria. Dealing with missing data We will contact the corresponding author or sponsor for additional or unpublished data in a study (e.g. dropout, lost to follow‐up, or when a study is published as an abstract only) as needed. A reminder email will be sent after two weeks. We will include any data obtained through an author reply in the analysis. If we do not obtain data from study authors, we will perform analyses with the available data using the methods described in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Intervention s ( Deeks 2024 ). If a study does not report data in means and standard deviations, we will follow the methods described in the Cochrane Handbook to extract or estimate relevant data ( Deeks 2024 ). If data are not available in numerical form but are in graphical form, we will attempt to extract data from the figures. If we are unable to obtain missing data by any method, and missing data are thought to introduce serious bias as per RoB 2, we will conduct a sensitivity analysis using a best‐case scenario (participants with missing data in the intervention arm developed events of desirable outcomes, and participants with missing data in the control arm developed no event of a desirable outcome) and a worst‐case scenario (participants with missing data in the intervention arm developed events of undesirable outcomes, and participants with missing data in the control arm developed no event of undesirable outcome) (see Sensitivity analysis ). We will address the potential impact of missing data on the findings of the review in the Discussion section. Assessment of heterogeneity We will assess three types of heterogeneity: clinical, methodological, and statistical heterogeneity. We will consider participants' characteristics (age, gender, aetiology, etc.), intervention, outcome, and length of follow‐up in our assessment of clinical heterogeneity; study design (RCTs only) and risk of bias in our assessment of methodological heterogeneity; and the I 2 statistic in our assessment of statistical heterogeneity ( Higgins 2022 ; Higgins 2020 ). We will interpret the I 2 as follows ( Deeks 2024 ): 0% to 40%: might not be important; 30% to 60%: may represent moderate heterogeneity; 50% to 90%: may represent substantial heterogeneity; 75% to 100%: considerable heterogeneity. Assessment of reporting biases We will assess reporting bias using a funnel plot if the number of study reports is higher than 10 for a given outcome. We will visually inspect the funnel plot for asymmetries, which show possible publication bias and overestimation of treatment effect. Data synthesis We will combine study reports in the forest plot in the case of low clinical, methodological, and statistical heterogeneity. We will include all eligible studies irrespective of risk of bias judgements in the forest plot. We will use a random‐effects model for data synthesis. We will prepare forest plots in RevMan 2025 . In the case of considerable heterogeneity, we will not pool data in a forest plot. If meta‐analysis is not possible (e.g. no eligible studies, or lack of data), then we will present a narrative synthesis based on the Synthesis Without Meta‐analysis (SWiM) guidelines ( Campbell 2020 ). Subgroup analysis and investigation of heterogeneity If we suspect clinical heterogeneity and there is a sufficient number of studies (10 studies), we will perform subgroup analyses based on the following characteristics. Type of LWM Synthetic absorbable poliglecaprone or polyglactin versus synthetic non‐absorbable polypropylene Type of inguinal hernia Indirect, direct, femoral, or lateral/medial Primary or recurrent ( Miserez 2007 ) Size of the hernial defect, as defined in the European Hernia Society classification ( Miserez 2007 ) Type of hernia surgery: open or laparoscopic We will use the formal test to find subgroup differences in RevMan 2025 . We will compare the magnitude of the effect between subgroups by assessing the overlap of CIs of the summary estimate. CIs that do not overlap indicate evidence of an effect. Sensitivity analysis We will perform the following sensitivity analyses. RCTs: by removing studies judged to be at high risk of bias or with some concerns. Differences in participant characteristics: absence or presence of comorbidities ( HerniaSurge Group 2018 ); clinical or radiological hernia ( HerniaSurge Group 2018 ); absence or presence of giant scrotal hernias ( Tran 2023 ). Studies where missing data were imputed: we will perform sensitivity analysis by excluding any such studies. This applies to binary outcomes. Summary of findings and assessment of the certainty of the evidence We will use GRADEpro GDT to present the following prioritised outcomes in the summary of findings table and to assess the certainty of the evidence. Chronic pain measured on a VAS beyond three months postoperatively. Hernia recurrence (clinical) within three months. Quality of life using HerQLes, preoperatively and postoperatively as mentioned in the included studies at one year of repair. Surgical‐site infections (clinical) within 30 days of repair. Haematoma/seroma within 30 days of repair. Two review authors (AKP and BPS) will independently assess the certainty of evidence. In case of discrepancy, the decision of a third review author (AK) will be final. We will assess the certainty of evidence based on the five GRADE considerations (risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias). The overall risk of bias judgement will inform the GRADE assessment. We will summarise risk of bias data before deciding to downgrade the certainty of evidence as per GRADE recommendations ( Schünemann 2023 ), and three possible categories will be: low risk of bias (when most information about an outcome is from studies at low risk of bias); moderate risk of bias (when most information about an outcome is from studies at low risk of bias or with some concerns); and high risk of bias (when most information about an outcome is from studies at high risk of bias which is sufficient to affect the interpretation of results). On the basis of these parameters, we may downgrade the certainty of evidence for the above outcomes by one or two levels per GRADE recommendations ( Schünemann 2023 ). We will support all judgements about the certainty of evidence using footnotes. The findings and certainty of evidence will be phrased according to the informative statement guidance ( Santesso 2020 ). We are grateful to the editorial base of Cochrane Colorectal for their suggestions to improve the protocol. documents.title: Assessing the utility of fractional excretion of urea in distinguishing intrinsic and prerenal acute kidney injury in hospitalised patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a significant challenge in hospital settings, and accurately differentiating between intrinsic and prerenal AKI is crucial for effective management. The fractional excretion of urea (FEUN) has been proposed as a potential biomarker for this purpose, offering an alternative to traditional markers such as fractional excretion of sodium. This study aimed to assess the diagnostic accuracy of FEUN for differentiating intrinsic from prerenal AKI in hospitalised patients.
DESIGNS: We conducted a systematic review and bivariate random effects meta-analysis of diagnostic accuracy studies. The study followed the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach.
DATA SOURCES: PubMed, Embase and Cochrane databases were searched from inception to 1 November 2023.
ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA FOR SELECTING STUDIES: We included observational studies that focused on patient with AKI and reported FEUN data sufficient to reconstruct a complete 2 × 2 contingency table (true positives, true negatives, false positives and false negatives) for evaluating its diagnostic accuracy.
DATA EXTRACTION AND SYNTHESIS: Two reviewers extracted data, assessed risk of bias with Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 and graded certainty of evidence using the GRADE approach. Pooled sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative likelihood ratios, and the area under the summary receiver operating characteristic curve (SROC) were calculated; heterogeneity was measured with I². A prespecified subgroup restricted to patients receiving diuretics served as a sensitivity analysis.
RESULTS: 12 studies involving 1240 patients were included, with an overall occurrence rate of intrinsic AKI of 38.8%. FEUN had a pooled sensitivity of 0.74 (95% CI 0.60 to 0.84) and specificity of 0.78 (95% CI 0.66 to 0.87), with positive predictive value and negative predictive value of 0.76 (95% CI 0.68 to 0.83) and 0.74 (95% CI 0.66 to 0.81), respectively. The SROC curve showed a pooled diagnostic accuracy of 0.83. Heterogeneity was substantial (I²>90%) for sensitivity and specificity. In a diuretic-only subgroup (six studies) specificity rose to 0.87 and heterogeneity declined (I²=56%). Overall certainty of evidence was low owing to inconsistency.
CONCLUSIONS: FEUN is a biomarker with moderate diagnostic accuracy for differentiating between intrinsic and prerenal AKI in hospitalised patients. Its application could enhance AKI management; however, the high heterogeneity observed in our study highlights the need for further research to evaluate its utility across diverse patient populations and clinical settings.
PROSPERO REGISTRATION NUMBER: CRD42024496083.

FEUN demonstrated moderate and consistent diagnostic performance, including in patients receiving diuretics, supporting its use when sodium-based indices are unreliable. Introduction Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common and complex condition affecting a significant proportion of hospitalised patients, particularly those in critical care, with an incidence ranging from 40% to 70%. 1 AKI leads to an extended hospital stay and higher healthcare costs, and it is also associated with a mortality rate of 10–20%. 2 Moreover, AKI significantly increases the risk of subsequent health complications, including cardiovascular diseases, hypertension, chronic kidney disease (CKD), end-stage renal disease and mortality. 3 7 The prompt recognition of AKI is crucial, as it enables timely interventions that can markedly improve patient outcomes. 8 9 AKI manifests across a broad spectrum of clinical scenarios, each requiring tailored management and intervention strategies. Crucially, the ability to differentiate between its primary causes—namely intrinsic (resulting from direct kidney damage) and prerenal (resulting from inadequate kidney perfusion)—is essential for guiding treatment choices, forecasting outcomes and providing patient education. 10 The traditional approach to differentiating these conditions primarily relies on clinical assessment, renal ultrasound and biochemical markers, including the fractional excretion of sodium (FENa). However, the use of FENa can be limited by factors such as the use of diuretics, a common treatment in hospital settings, which reduces sodium reabsorption and consequently elevates the levels of FENa. 11 12 This limitation has prompted the search for alternative tools that can provide accurate diagnostic information without being significantly affected by therapeutic interventions. In this context, the fractional excretion of urea (FEUN) relies mainly on passive forces, making it less susceptible to the effects of diuretics. This attribute potentially makes FEUN a useful adjunct test for distinguishing between intrinsic and prerenal AKI. For comparison, a previous systematic review showed that FENa yields pooled sensitivity of 0.64 and specificity of 0.71. 11 The rationale of using FEUN is based on the differential handling of urea in conditions of altered renal perfusion compared with intrinsic renal damage. In prerenal AKI, where there is a physiological response to conserve sodium, urea reabsorption is also enhanced, leading to a lower FEUN. Conversely, in intrinsic AKI, the renal tubules’ capacity to reabsorb urea is impaired, resulting in a higher FEUN level. 13 Despite its theoretical advantages, the clinical application of FEUN and its effectiveness in differentiating AKI aetiologies in hospitalised patients remains an area of active investigation. 14 16 Previous studies have reported mixed results, with variations in sensitivity, specificity and overall diagnostic accuracy. 12 17 18 These discrepancies may be attributed to differences in study populations, the criteria used to define AKI and the presence of confounding clinical conditions. Given the potential of FEUN to improve the diagnostic approach to AKI, a systematic review and meta-analysis of the available literature is warranted. Therefore, we conducted this study to assess the utility of FEUN in distinguishing between intrinsic and prerenal AKI among hospitalised patients, synthesising evidence from diverse clinical settings to provide a comprehensive evaluation of its diagnostic performance. We aimed to clarify the role of FEUN in clinical practice, offering insights that could inform both clinical decision-making and guidelines for AKI management. Methods Ethics statement This investigation synthesised data already published in peer-reviewed journals and did not involve contact with patients, use of identifiable information or any new experiments on humans or animals. In accordance with the regulations of the Institutional Review Board of Chang Gung Memorial Hospital and the Declaration of Helsinki, such secondary analyses are exempt from formal review and informed consent requirements. Consequently, no ethics approval was sought or required. Data sources and search strategies Three investigators (Z-HJ, H-CP and H-YC) independently conducted a thorough search of PubMed, Embase and Cochrane databases from inception to 1 November 2023. No language restrictions were set, and the target was observational studies evaluating the efficacy of FEUN. The search terms were “acute kidney injury” and “fractional excretion of urea”, along with relevant MeSH or Emtree terms, and keywords synonymous or related to the topic. Details of the search syntax, database coverage and two-stage screening procedure are provided in online supplemental appendices 1 and 2 . Our methodology aligned with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses statement ( online supplemental appendix 3 ). 19 In addition, we registered the protocol of this systematic review and meta-analysis with the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO, registration number CRD42024496083, online supplemental appendix 4 ). This study is a systematic review and meta-analysis of previously published data and does not involve human participants or identifiable personal information. Therefore, ethical approval was not required. Inclusion and exclusion criteria There were no restrictions on study design. Eligible studies had to (1) include participants aged 18 years or older; (2) confirm a diagnosis of AKI; (3) studies that reported, or provided sufficient data to reconstruct, a complete 2 × 2 contingency table (true positives (TP), true negatives (TN), false positives (FP) and false negatives (FN)) for FEUN diagnostic accuracy. Studies were excluded if they (1) lacked details on outcomes of interest; (2) provided insufficient data to calculate TP, TN, FP and FN for FEUN; (3) had no English language full text or English translation containing the necessary data; (4) were editorial, conference, review articles; and (5) were animal and in vitro studies. Study selection and data extraction Two reviewers (Z-HJ and C-CH) independently screened titles/abstracts and, subsequently, full texts; a third author (H-YC) resolved disagreements. A detailed description of the two-stage screening workflow, deduplication software and manual reference checking appears in the ‘Data sources and search strategies’ subsection and is illustrated in figure 1 . Figure 1 The forest plot for evaluating the pooled sensitivity and specificity of FEUN in predicting intrinsic AKI. AKI, acute kidney injury; FEUN, fractional excretion of urea. For each eligible article, we extracted study characteristics, patient demographics, AKI definitions, FEUN measurement details and the full 2 × 2 contingency table (TP, TN, FP, FN) used for diagnostic pooling ( table 1 ). When derivation and validation cohorts were reported together, only the derivation cohort was used to avoid unit-of-analysis errors. All extracted information was cross-checked by a second reviewer, with any discrepancies adjudicated by H-CP and V-CW.
