Objectives This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review (intervention). The objectives are as follows: To assess the beneficial and harmful effects of sorafenib, with or without co‐interventions, versus placebo, no intervention, or the same co‐interventions for adults, aged 18 and over, with hepatocellular carcinoma. status released display-pdf yes is-olf no is-manuscript no is-preprint no is-journal-matter no is-scanned no is-retracted no Collection date 2025. Background Description of the condition Primary liver cancer is the sixth most common cancer, and the third leading cause of cancer death worldwide, with approximately 906,000 new primary liver cancers and 830,000 deaths in 2020 ( Sung 2021 ). The incidence and mortality of liver cancer have continuously risen during recent years ( Siegel 2023 ; Sung 2021 ). Globally, hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the dominant histological subtype of primary liver cancer, accounting for 75% to 85% of all primary liver cancers ( McGlynn 2021 ; Petrick 2020 ; Sung 2021 ). Seventy‐two per cent of HCCs occur in Asia (more than 50% in China), 10% in Europe, 7.8% in Africa, 5.1% in North America, 4.6% in Latin America, and 0.5% in Oceania ( Singal 2020 ). The development of HCC is attributable to several causative factors and underlying liver diseases, including hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, alcohol use, and non‐alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD – recently called metabolic dysfunction‐associated steatohepatitis (MASH)) ( Llovet 2021a ; McGlynn 2021 ; Singal 2020 ; Vogel 2022 ). In Africa and East Asia, the largest attributable fraction is HBV (60%), while in the Western world, chronic HCV is the most common underlying liver disease aetiology ( Akinyemiju 2017 ; Singal 2020 ). Hepatocarcinogenesis is closely correlated with cirrhosis, which develops in chronic liver diseases, increasing the risk of the development of HCC. However, HCC can also develop in a non‐cirrhotic liver. Regional differences and environmental factors may lead to a higher frequency of HCC in people with liver diseases without cirrhosis ( Yang 2019 ). Age, male sex, smoking, obesity, metabolic syndrome, and diabetes mellitus are also risk factors for HCC ( Llovet 2021a ; McGlynn 2021 ; Vogel 2022 ). Exposure to aflatoxin B1 is especially relevant in Asia and Sub‐Saharan Africa ( Chen 2022 ; Williams 2004 ). Usually, HCC has a silent onset with no symptoms in the early stages. Some non‐specific symptoms may occur when HCC progresses to the intermediate and advanced stages, including malaise, weight loss, anorexia, nausea, abdominal discomfort, reduced performance, or signs related to advanced liver dysfunction. Alpha‐fetoprotein (AFP) is the most common surveillance serum biomarker for HCC ( Daniele 2004 ; Marrero 2020 ). Abdominal ultrasonography is an imaging modality recommended for screening for HCC ( Daniele 2004 ; Marrero 2020 ). HCC can be diagnosed based on validated imaging criteria in people with liver cirrhosis or tissue biopsy ( El‐Serag 2008 ; Llovet 2021a ; Vogel 2022 ). The Child‐Pugh score was introduced in 1973 as a prognostic indicator for liver cirrhosis, to evaluate liver function ( Pugh 1973 ). Many studies have affirmed the prognostic importance of the Child‐Pugh score in HCC, and incorporated it into staging systems as an important consideration in formulating treatment strategies ( Duseja 2014 ; Vogel 2023 ). Several classifications have been proposed for people with HCC, amongst which, the Barcelona Clinic of Liver Cancer (BCLC) algorithm is the most widely used staging system, as it links the prognosis of HCC with the best treatment options, based on strong clinical evidence ( Llovet 2021a ; Reig 2022 ; Vogel 2022 ). Based on tumour burden (tumour number, tumour size, vascular invasion, and extrahepatic spread), liver function (Child‐Pugh score), and performance status (Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance Status (ECOG PS)), the BCLC staging system subdivides people with HCC into five clinical stages: very early stage (BCLC‐0), early stage (BCLC‐A), intermediate stage (BCLC‐B), advanced stage (BCLC‐C), and terminal stage (BCLC‐D). With the progress of medical technology, surgical resection, liver transplantation, ablation, transarterial chemoembolisation (TACE), and sorafenib have been developed and optimised for people with HCC who have different prognoses ( Llovet 2021a ; Vogel 2022 ; Yang 2020a ). Description of the intervention Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) TKIs are a class of compounds that can suppress the growth and metastasis of tumour cells by inhibiting the phosphorylation of tyrosine residues in proteins and blocking the downstream signal pathways ( Du 2018 ; Tan 2018 ). With the advantages of multiple targets, limited adverse effects, and significant efficacy, TKIs have exhibited promise in the systemic treatment of HCC ( Da Fonseca 2020 ). Representative drugs include sorafenib, lenvatinib, regorafenib, and cabozantinib. Sorafenib was approved as a first‐line treatment for HCC in 2007 ( Di Marco 2013 ). It remained the standard of care and the only first‐line systemic therapy for advanced HCC for over a decade, until the emergence of lenvatinib as an alternative first‐line option, and later, combination therapies (e.g. atezolizumab + bevacizumab) ( Di Marco 2013 ; Llovet 2021a ; Vogel 2022 ). Sorafenib exerts anti‐proliferative and anti‐angiogenic effects by targeting the rapidly accelerated fibrosarcoma (RAF)/mitogen‐activated protein (MAP)/extracellular signal‐regulated kinase (ERK) kinase (MEK)/ERK cascade, the vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGFR), the platelet‐derived growth factor receptor (PDGFR), and more ( Galmiche 2014 ). The median overall survival of people treated with sorafenib improved in phase Ⅲ trials (SHARP and Asia‐Pacific) ( Cheng 2009 ; Llovet 2008 ; Rimassa 2009 ). The survival benefit of sorafenib was further confirmed in multiple subsequent studies ( Bruix 2012 ; Iavarone 2011 ; Marrero 2016 ). In a recent meta‐analysis including 13, mainly observational, studies, better overall survival and recurrence‐free survival were found in the adjuvant sorafenib group compared to the observational or placebo groups ( Huang 2021 ). Combined data also revealed that people treated with sorafenib after resection had a lower recurrence rate ( Huang 2021 ). A non‐Cochrane systematic review compared the efficacy of sorafenib combined with local therapies (external radiotherapy, TACE, or hepatic artery infusion chemotherapy) with sorafenib as monotherapy for the treatment of unresectable HCC ( Li 2023 ). The combined results found that the combination of sorafenib and local therapy was associated with better overall survival than monotherapy ( Li 2023 ). However, both sorafenib alone and sorafenib combined with local treatments seem to cause several adverse events ( Gyawali 2017 ; Li 2023 ; Long 2023 ; Shen 2013 ). Child‐Pugh class and ECOG PS scores should be considered during sorafenib therapy ( Baek 2011 ; Tsukui 2012 ). A study that assessed sorafenib efficacy and safety in SHARP‐eligible and non‐eligible participants, supported restricting sorafenib usage to people categorised as Child‐Pugh A ( Labeur 2018 ). However, in a meta‐analysis, the response rates, safety, and tolerability of sorafenib did not differ by Child‐Pugh class ( McNamara 2018 ). At present, sorafenib remains the first‐line treatment for people with Child‐Pugh class A, and ECOG PS 0‐1 advanced HCC, especially when there are contraindications for the use of atezolizumab + bevacizumab or durvalumab + tremelimumab (Evidence quality: moderate; Strength of recommendation: strong ( Gordan 2024 )). Surgical resection Surgical resection, performed via open or laparoscopic approaches, involves the complete removal of HCC plus a safety margin of non‐tumorous liver parenchyma to achieve a radical cure ( Cauchy 2014 ; Orcutt 2018 ). Its mechanism relies on anatomical dissection, guided by intraoperative ultrasound and vascular control techniques, to physically eliminate malignant tissue while preserving sufficient functional liver volume ( Lau 2010 ; Makuuchi 1998 ). As a first‐line curative treatment, resection is recommended for early‐stage HCC (BCLC‐0/A) and selected intermediate‐stage cases (BCLC‐B) in people with preserved liver function (Child‐Pugh A), as it demonstrates better long‐term oncologic outcomes than local ablation ( Reig 2022 ; Shin 2021 ; Yeo 2024 ; Yin 2018 ; Zhaohui 2019 ). Innovations, such as laparoscopic/robotic resection, have shown reductions in hospital stay and rate of complications compared to open surgery ( Ciria 2016 ; Ciria 2022 ). Advanced preoperative planning, using three‐dimensional reconstruction visualisation technology, has significantly improved the perioperative outcomes for people with HCC ( Zeng 2024 ), while combined strategies, like liver partition plus portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS), enable resection in a considerable proportion of people with an insufficient future liver remnant ( Vennarecci 2016 ; Wang 2020 ). Despite challenges, including high recurrence rates and limited applicability in advanced cirrhosis, resection remains the cornerstone of HCC management, due to its radical tumour clearance, pathological staging utility, and compatibility with adjuvant therapies. Thermal ablation Thermal ablation is usually performed under imaging guidance, with a thin needle that is placed through the skin (percutaneously) into the tumour, to release heat or cold energy and cause irreversible cell death ( Crocetti 2008 ; Goldberg 2003 ). The techniques of thermal ablation mainly include radiofrequency ablation (RFA), microwave ablation (MWA), laser ablation, ultrasound ablation, and cryoablation. RFA and MWA work by converting electrical currents and electromagnetic waves into heat ( Buscarini 2005 ; Simon 2005 ). Laser ablation destroys the tumour by direct heating with laser beams ( Vogl 2006 ). Ultrasound ablation focusses ultrasonic beams on the target regions to induce a thermal effect and a cavitation effect ( Yang 1993 ). Cryoablation causes tissue injury through a process of freezing and rewarming ( Niu 2014 ). Both RFA and MWA have shown survival benefits for HCC ( Zhu 2019 ). According to the BCLC staging system and treatment recommendations, ablation is suitable for HCC in very early (BCLC‐0) or early (BCLC‐A) stages ( EASL 2018 ; Reig 2022 ). It has been reported that people with HCC receiving ablation have a similar prognosis as those receiving resection, especially in early‐stage HCC ( Livraghi 2008 ). Recently, percutaneous ablation was considered to reduce the risk of treatment changes from curative strategies to palliative strategies ( Zhou 2021 ). In recently published studies, the application of percutaneous ablation in HCC management has exceeded the recommendations of the BCLC staging system and treatment strategy, achieving effective local tumour control ( Ho 2014 ; Nault 2018 ; Renzulli 2020 ; Zhou 2021 ). With the advancement of technological innovations and the application of combined therapeutic strategies, encouraging results of ablation techniques have been shown in the treatment of people with HCC at intermediate (BCLC‐B) or advanced (BCLC‐C) stages, and in the treatment of unfavourable tumour locations ( Iezzi 2016 ; Renzulli 2020 ). Considering the advantages of minimal invasiveness, more repeatability, and fewer complications, thermal ablation has gained increasing importance in HCC management ( Maruyama 2023 ; Serbanescu‐Kele Apor de Zalán 2022 ; Weis 2013 ; Xu 2022 ). Transarterial chemoembolisation (TACE) TACE is an image‐guided interventional procedure that selectively delivers chemotherapeutic agents, combined with embolic particles, into the tumour‐feeding hepatic arteries, inducing ischaemic necrosis and localised drug cytotoxicity. The mechanism involves dual effects: (1) obstruction of arterial blood flow to starve the tumour, and (2) sustained intratumoural drug release to enhance cytotoxicity. Conventional TACE (cTACE) utilises lipiodol‐chemotherapy emulsions followed by particle embolisation, while drug‐eluting bead TACE (DEB‐TACE) employs microspheres preloaded with doxorubicin, or other agents, for controlled drug release ( Chang 2020 ; Raoul 2019 ). According to BCLC guidelines, TACE serves as the standard of care for intermediate‐stage HCC (BCLC‐B) with multifocal lesions and preserved liver function, achieving a median survival of more than 26 months to 30 months ( EASL 2018 ; Llovet 2021a ). Recent studies demonstrate expanded applications, including downstaging advanced HCC for curative therapies ( Zhao 2023 ), and bridging therapy before liver transplantation ( Viveiros 2019 ). Combination strategies with ablation or systemic therapies have improved objective response rates and survival rates ( Wang 2024 ; Yuan 2021 ; Zhang 2022 ). Technological advances, such as cone‐beam CT guidance and radiation‐emitting microspheres, enhance tumour targeting while reducing off‐target embolisation ( Bucalau 2021 ; Jiang 2024 ). Despite its minimally invasive nature and repeatability, limitations include incomplete necrosis and risk of liver function deterioration in people classed as Child‐Pugh B or C. Ongoing innovations in personalised embolisation protocols and biomarker‐driven selection aim to optimise therapeutic efficacy ( Wu 2025 ; Zhu 2025 ). Other locoregional therapies Other locoregional therapies include ethanol injection, hepatic artery infusion chemotherapy (HAIC), and radiotherapy. Ethanol injection, a minimally invasive technique, induces tumour necrosis through direct chemical ablation, achieving a local recurrence rate at three years of 10% in small (≤ 3 cm diameter) HCC tumours ( Ebara 2005 ). HAIC administers concentrated chemotherapeutic agents directly into tumour‐feeding arteries via implanted catheters, showing better efficacy against HCC with portal vein tumour thrombosis than sorafenib ( Zhang 2023 ). Radiotherapy, particularly stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT), delivers precise high‐dose radiation to tumours while sparing healthy parenchyma. Published data demonstrate its association with excellent local control and survival rates in people with HCC, particularly those who are unsuitable for, or refractory to, standard locoregional therapies ( Keane 2016 ; Mathew 2020 ). Immunotherapy, including PD‐1/PD‐L1 inhibitors, has revolutionised systemic treatment, with objective response rates of 20% in advanced HCC ( El‐Khoueiry 2017 ). Conventional chemotherapy remains limited to a select HCC population, demonstrating modest survival benefits in China ( Qin 2014 ; Qin 2016 ). Recent advancements include combined radiotherapy and immunotherapy to enhance abscopal effects ( Choi 2019 ; Nahm 2023 ; Nakabori 2024 ; Yoo 2021 ), HAIC‐sorafenib synergism for macrovascular invasion ( Ueshima 2020 ), and biomarker‐guided immunotherapeutic strategies ( Yang 2020b ; Zhou 2018 ). While these therapies expand options for intermediate‐advanced HCC, challenges persist in optimising sequencing, managing toxicity, and validating predictive biomarkers. How the intervention might work HCC management requires multimodal approaches, due to its complex pathogenesis and high recurrence rates. While surgical resection, thermal ablation, TACE, and systemic therapies each have established roles, their standalone use often yields suboptimal outcomes. For instance, locoregional therapies, like TACE or ablation, may fail to control microscopic residual tumours ( Huang 2000 ; Zhang 2019 ), while systemic therapies alone may struggle to address macroscopic tumour burden effectively. Emerging evidence supports the rationale for combining sorafenib with other interventions to target complementary pathways and improve clinical outcomes ( Huang 2021 ; Long 2023 ; Zeng 2023 ). When combined with other interventions, sorafenib may act synergistically by: (1) preventing post‐treatment recurrence: adjuvant sorafenib after resection or ablation could suppress micrometastases and residual tumour cells ( Kong 2016 ; Shi 2013 ; Wu 2021 ); (2) enhancing disease control: concurrent use with TACE may counteract hypoxia‐induced VEGF upregulation post‐embolisation, potentially delaying tumour revascularisation ( Omyła‐Staszewska 2012 ; Petrillo 2018 ); (3) overcoming therapeutic resistance: sequential or combined regimens might overcome intrinsic resistance to single‐modality therapy ( Chen 2016 ; Cheng 2022 ; Huang 2013 ). Sorafenib improves overall survival and enhances disease control compared with placebo in systematic reviews of randomised clinical trials ( Haber 2021 ; Shen 2013 ). Some studies have reported the combination of sorafenib and local therapy ( Chapiro 2014 ; Kudo 2020 ; Ricke 2019 ; Rim 2021 ; Seidensticker 2023 ). TACE combined with sorafenib provided a better objective response rate (risk ratio (RR) = 1.62), disease control rate (RR = 1.43), 0.5‐year overall survival rate (odds ratio (OR) = 2.60), and 1‐year overall survival rate (OR = 1.88) for people with advanced HCC than TACE alone ( Cai 2017 ). Zhang and colleagues also confirmed that combination therapy was better than TACE alone ( Zhang 2020 ). An umbrella review found that TACE plus sorafenib enhanced survival and tumour response, but there was also a higher incidence of adverse events ( Yan 2023 ). Adjuvant sorafenib therapy after resection in people with HCC was also observed to have a significant association with better overall survival and recurrence‐free survival, but without intolerable adverse effects, based mainly on observational evidence ( Huang 2021 ). In a retrospective study, adjuvant sorafenib following radiofrequency ablation (RFA) was associated with better survival in people with early‐stage recurrent HCC with microvascular invasion (MVI) at the initial hepatectomy ( Wei 2022 ). A recent observational study assessed the efficacy of RFA plus sorafenib versus RFA alone. Combined therapy improved the total effective rate and the one‐, two‐, and three‐year survival rates ( Yang 2024 ). STORM, a phase 3, randomised, double‐blind, placebo‐controlled trial, was designed to assess the efficacy and safety of sorafenib as adjuvant therapy versus placebo in people with HCC after surgical resection or local ablation ( Bruix 2015 ). However, there was no observed difference in median recurrence‐free survival between the two groups. A recent randomised trial compared TACE plus sorafenib with TACE alone in people with recurrent intermediate‐stage HCC, post‐R0 hepatectomy. They found a significantly higher median overall survival of 22.2 months for the combination therapy versus 15.1 months for TACE alone ( Fan 2024 ). Investigations are currently underway to explore combinations of sorafenib with radiotherapy or hepatic artery infusion chemotherapy, providing greater hope for improved survival rates amongst people with liver cancer ( Chen 2023 ; He 2019 ; Li 2023 ). It is crucial to emphasise that the application of sorafenib in various populations can be influenced by several factors, such as the person's age, liver function, tumour burden, and existing health conditions ( Cabibbo 2013 ; Liu 2020 ; Pinyol 2019 ; Yang 2024 ). Older people often show significant differences in how well they tolerate treatments and manage adverse effects compared to younger people, which can affect both the choice of therapy and its effectiveness ( Cabibbo 2013 ). People with diabetes mellitus and hypertension may also face different prognoses following treatment ( Hsieh 2020 ; Rose 2024 ). Critical to optimising these combinations is the person's stratification. In summary, sorafenib, used alone or as part of multimodal regimens, targets multiple hallmarks of HCC progression. Combination therapy with sorafenib helps overcome the shortcomings of single treatments by precisely controlling when and where they act to influence tumour behaviour. Heterogeneous trial outcomes suggest the potential importance of personalised strategies, guided by tumour biology and host factors. Why it is important to do this review As one of the most common malignancies of the digestive system, HCC is characterised by high incidence and mortality ( McGlynn 2021 ; Siegel 2025 ). Much effort has been made to find a way to decrease the recurrence rate and improve the survival prognosis of people with HCC. While surgical resection, thermal ablation, and TACE are established locoregional therapies, systemic therapies, like sorafenib, have become integral to comprehensive treatment strategies ( Brown 2023 ; Vogel 2022 ; Zhong 2025 ). Sorafenib is the anti‐liver cancer TKI drug that has been used for the longest time and in the widest range of clinical presentations. Therefore, it has the most abundant data. Present studies are increasingly exploring the efficacy and safety of sorafenib with or without co‐interventions. The benefits of sorafenib, with or without co‐interventions, must be weighed against potential adverse effects. Some studies suggest synergistic effects when sorafenib is combined with locoregional therapies ( Huang 2021 ; Long 2023 ; Zeng 2023 ). Abdel‐Rahman and colleagues conducted a systematic review to explore the value of using a sorafenib‐based combination for advanced HCC. The results suggested that sorafenib, combined with some anticancer agents, could be a promising, effective, and tolerable treatment ( Abdel‐Rahman 2014 ). In 2019, a non‐Cochrane systematic review and meta‐analysis of 11 trials found that sorafenib, as a first‐line therapy for unresectable HCC, improved overall survival, but was ineffective as a second‐line or adjuvant therapy, and did not enhance TACE efficacy ( Huang 2019 ). Another non‐Cochrane systematic review and meta‐analysis, from 2024, evaluated the risks and benefits of TKIs for HCC. It found that TKI treatment improved survival and tumour response better than placebo. Combined TKI showed better objective response rates and minimal heterogeneity; but some gastrointestinal and neurological adverse events were noted ( Payo‐Serafín 2024 ). Overall, TKI therapy shows clinical benefits for advanced HCC, warranting its continued use while managing toxicity. Existing systematic reviews and meta‐analyses focused narrowly on specific combinations, failed to account for heterogeneity in co‐interventions, or did not include all well‐structured, high‐quality randomised clinical trials, which may significantly affect the results and conclusions drawn from the analyses ( Guyatt 2011 ; Thompson 1994 ). Clear and convincing evidence on the beneficial and harmful effects of sorafenib, with or without co‐interventions, for HCC is still lacking. A rigorous synthesis of the evidence is important to inform guidelines on treatment decisions, population selection, and safety monitoring. Using rigorous Cochrane methods, we intend to comprehensively evaluate the efficacy and safety of sorafenib across all therapeutic contexts, and provide the best certainty of evidence for the role of sorafenib, with or without co‐interventions, for people with HCC, regardless of tumour stage. Objectives To assess the beneficial and harmful effects of sorafenib, with or without co‐interventions, versus placebo, no intervention, or the same co‐interventions for adults, aged 18 and over, with hepatocellular carcinoma. Methods Criteria for considering studies for this review Types of studies We will include randomised controlled trials (RCTs) with a parallel‐group design, regardless of language, format, publication status, or outcomes reported. Trials with a cluster‐randomised or a cross‐over design are unlikely to have been performed for the topic of our review. We will exclude quasi‐randomised studies, as the allocation sequence generation can be anticipated by alternation, date of birth, day of admission, or medical record number ( Lefebvre 2025 ). Types of participants We will include adults aged 18 years and over, of any gender, race, or ethnicity, with histologically or radiologically diagnosed hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), regardless of the tumour stage, or the setting (primary care, hospital, or community). We will include trials with subsets of participants, i.e. with HCC and another liver disease, if at least 20% of the total number of included trial participants are diagnosed with HCC, and their data are presented separately from the irrelevant subset(s) of participants. We will contact trial authors for the missing data. If no reply is received, we will exclude the trial. Types of interventions We will include trials with these comparisons. Sorafenib versus placebo or no intervention Sorafenib with surgical resection versus surgical resection with placebo or no intervention Sorafenib with any thermal ablation technique versus the same thermal ablation technique with placebo or no intervention Sorafenib with transarterial chemoembolisation versus transarterial chemoembolisation with placebo or no intervention Sorafenib with any other drug versus the same drug (e.g. doxorubicin, capecitabine, everolimus, tigatuzumab, etc.) with placebo or no intervention Sorafenib with any other hepatocellular cancer intervention (e.g. ethanol injection) versus the same intervention (i.e. ethanol injection) with placebo or no intervention Co‐interventions We will consider trials with co‐interventions if they are administered equally to all trial groups. Types of outcome measures We will include relevant trials regardless of reported outcomes. We aim to assess the following outcomes up to six months after the first treatment, up to 12 months after the first treatment, and at the longest follow‐up (the exact time points are provided after each outcome below). We will use the outcome data reported at the longest follow‐up for our primary analyses. We consider the longest follow‐up time points as most clinically relevant for clinicians and people with HCC. Primary outcomes All‐cause mortality at the longest follow‐up . If data on all‐cause mortality are not reported, we will assess overall survival at the longest follow‐up. If trials report Kaplan‐Meier curves, we will follow Tierney's method to extract hazard ratios (HRs) from these trials ( Tierney 2007 ). Proportion of participants with one or more serious adverse events . Serious adverse events are defined by the International Conference on Harmonisation Guidelines for Good Clinical Practice as any untoward medical occurrence that results in death, is life‐threatening, requires inpatient hospitalisation or prolongation of existing hospitalisation, results in persistent or significant disability/incapacity, or a congenital anomaly/birth defect ( ICH 2016 ). All other adverse events will be considered non‐serious adverse events. We will assess adverse events up to 12 months after the first treatment and at the longest follow‐up. Quality of life , measured by validated questionnaires, e.g. World Health Organisation Quality of Life (WHOQOL) ( WHO 1995 ), European Quality of Life (EuroQol)‐5 Dimension (EQ‐5D) ( Rabin 2001 ), 36‐item Short Form Health Survey (SF‐36) ( Ware 1992 ), European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer Quality of Life Questionnaire (EORTC QLQ‐C30) ( Aaronson 1993 ), and Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy scale (FACT‐G) ( Cella 1993 ). If trials use and report more than one scale for quality of life, we will use data from the questionnaires in this sequence: the WHOQOL questionnaire; EQ‐5D questionnaire, SF‐36, EORTC QLQ‐C30, and the FACT‐G questionnaire. We will assess quality of life up to 12 months after the first treatment and at the longest follow‐up. Secondary outcomes Progression‐free survival: measured as the time from the first treatment to disease progression or death caused by any reason, whichever happens first, or the longest follow‐up Recurrence‐free survival : measured as the time from the first treatment to HCC recurrence or death caused by any reason, whichever happens first, or the longest follow‐up Proportion of participants with objective response rate (ORR) : measured as the proportion of participants with complete response (CR) and partial response (PR), up to six months after the first treatment Proportion of participants with one or more non‐serious adverse events , i.e. not included in the definition of serious adverse events, or as defined by the trial authors; measured up to 12 months after the first treatment, and at the longest follow‐up Proportion of participants with complete response (CR) : defined as the disappearance of any intratumoural arterial enhancement in all target lesions; measured up to six months after the first treatment Proportion of participants with partial response (PR) : defined as at least a 30% decrease in the sum of diameters of viable (enhancement in the arterial phase) target lesions, using the baseline sum of the diameters of target lesions as the reference point; measured up to six months after the first treatment Proportion of participants with progressive disease (PD) : defined as an increase of at least 20% in the sum of the diameters of viable (enhancing) target lesions, using the smallest sum of the diameters of viable (enhancing) target lesions recorded since treatment started as the reference point; measured up to six months after the first treatment Proportion of participants with stable disease (SD) : defined as any participant who does not qualify for either partial response or progressive disease; measured up to six months after the first treatment We consider the Modified Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours (mRECIST) guidelines to be the main HCC evaluation tool ( Lencioni 2010 ), since it has become the standard tool for radiological evaluation of HCC response in clinical practice ( Gregory 2020 ; Kim 2015 ; Llovet 2020 ). Whenever appropriate, we will also consider other criteria, such as the World Health Organization (WHO) criteria ( Kim 2015 ), and the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours (RECIST) guidelines ( Therasse 2000 ). Search methods for identification of studies To minimise bias in our search results, we followed the guidance in Chapter 4 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions ( Lefebvre 2025 ), and the PRISMA‐S (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta‐Analyses literature search extension) checklist (PRISMA-S Checklist; Rethlefsen 2021 ), to plan and describe the search process for the review. The Cochrane Hepato‐Biliary Group (CHBG) Information Specialist developed the search strategies and will perform the electronic searches. Electronic searches We will search for randomised clinical trials in: CHBG Controlled Trials Register, in the Cochrane Register of Studies Web (search date); Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL; current issue) in the Cochrane Library; MEDLINE ALL Ovid (1946 to present); Embase Ovid (Excerpta Medica Database; 1974 to present); LILACS (VHL Regional Portal; Latin American and Caribbean Health Science Information database; 1982 to present); Science Citation Index Expanded, and Conference Proceedings Citation Index ‐ Science (Web of Science; search date); The China National Knowledge Infrastructure database (CNKI) and Wanfang database will be searched in Chinese (search date). As described in Chapter 4 of the Cochrane Handbook, we will apply search filters where relevant ( Lefebvre 2025 ). We will also search for and examine any relevant retraction statements and errata for information ( Lefebvre 2024 ). We will do so by including relevant search terms for retractions and errata into the highly sensitive search strategies designed by Cochrane for identifying randomised clinical trials for the electronic searches of MEDLINE ALL Ovid and Embase Ovid ( Lefebvre 2024 ; Lefebvre 2025 ). Appendix 1 provides the search strategies for each database, with the expected date range of the searches. We will provide the actual dates of the electronic searches at the review stage. Searching other resources We will search the on‐line trial registries: US National Institutes of Health Ongoing Trials Register ClinicalTrials.gov (clinicaltrials.gov/); World Health Organization International Clinical Trial Registry Platform ( www.who.int/ictrp ); EU Clinical Trials Register ( www.clinicaltrialsregister.eu/ ); ISRCTN registry ( www.isrctn.com/ ); European Medicines Agency (EMA; www.ema.europa.eu/ema/ ); Food and Drug Administration (FDA; www.fda.gov ); Chinese Clinical Trial Register (ChiCTR; www.chictr.org.cn/ ); and pharmaceutical company sources for ongoing or unpublished trials, and for study information. We will also contact relevant individuals and organisations for information about unpublished or ongoing studies. We will search for relevant grey literature sources, such as reports, dissertations, theses, and conference abstracts, e.g. in Google Scholar. We will use the 'Similar articles' algorithmic function in MEDLINE to identify similar publications for included trials. We will also manually check citations and reference lists of the included trials, and any relevant systematic reviews identified. We will contact authors of identified trials for additional published or unpublished trials. At the review stage, we will describe in detail how the searches were performed and provide the most current search dates. We will use items from the PRISMA‐S checklist to ensure that we report and document our searches as advised (PRISMA-S Checklist; Rethlefsen 2021 ). Data collection and analysis We will follow the instructions in the Cochrane Handbook for data collection and analysis ( Higgins 2024a ). We will use Review Manager software to perform the meta‐analysis ( RevMan 2025 ). Selection of studies Two review authors (SC and XL) will independently select trials for inclusion, using Covidence . We will identify and exclude duplicate records not identified during the initial de‐duplication of the search results handled by the CHBG Information Specialist, using the Cochrane Register of Studies Web. We will screen the titles and abstracts of all unique records obtained by electronic and other source searches for potentially relevant trials. We will retrieve the full text of all relevant and potentially relevant records, and two review authors (SC and SD) will independently screen these to identify trials for inclusion. We will identify and record reasons for the exclusion of ineligible reports. We will correspond with study investigators as required, to clarify study eligibility. We will resolve any disagreement through discussion; if required, we will consult a third person (JPL). We will identify and collate multiple reports of the same study, so that each study, rather than each record, is the unit of interest in the review. We will record the selection process in sufficient detail to complete a PRISMA flow diagram ( Page 2021a ; Page 2021b ). For the screening of non‐Chinese and non‐English language publications, we will, in the first instance, use Google Translate to assist with the eligibility assessment (translate.google.com). If needed, we will seek translators through the CHBG to assist with assessing studies for potential eligibility; if eligible, we will request assistance with data extraction by native speakers. Data extraction and management We will create a data extraction form that we will pilot test on at least two trials, before embarking on data extraction. Two review authors (XL and SD) will independently extract study data as outlined below. Disagreements will be resolved through discussion; if needed, a third review author (WL) will be involved to resolve the disagreements. Methods: study design, total duration of study, study centres and location, study setting, and date of study Participants: number randomised, number lost to follow‐up/withdrawn, number analysed, mean age, age range, sex, ethnicity, severity of condition, aetiology, diagnostic criteria, Child‐Pugh grade of liver function, Barcelona Clinic of Liver Cancer (BCLC) stage, subsets of participants, inclusion criteria, and exclusion criteria Interventions: intervention, comparison, concomitant medications, and excluded medications. We will also extract information on trial groups. Outcomes: outcomes specified and collected, scales used, and time points reported Notes: trial protocol, funding of the trial, and notable conflicts of interest of trial authors, information on withdrawn trials or error messages In the characteristics of included studies table, we will note if outcome data were not reported in a usable way. We will resolve disagreements by consensus, involving all review authors. One review author (SC) will enter the data into the characteristics of included studies table. Another review author (XL) will check trial characteristics for accuracy against the trial reports. For multi‐arm trials, we will provide information on all trial groups, regardless of their relevance to our review. Assessment of risk of bias in included studies Two review authors (XL and SD) will independently assess the risk of bias in the included studies. We will resolve disagreements by discussion until consensus amongst all review authors is reached. We will assess the risk of bias using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool ( Higgins 2024b ; Sterne 2019 ). We will assess the effect of the 'assignment to the intervention'. In order to do this, we will use the intention‐to‐treat (ITT) principle, which includes all randomised participants, regardless of the interventions they actually received. We will assess the risk of bias based on the following domains ( Higgins 2024b ; Sterne 2019 ). Bias arising from the randomisation process: we will assess whether the allocation sequence was random and adequately concealed. We will also assess if the baseline differences between intervention groups suggest an issue with the randomisation process. Bias due to deviations from intended interventions: we will evaluate whether the participants were aware of their assigned interventions during the trial and if the carers and people delivering the interventions were aware of the participants' assigned intervention during the trial. Bias due to missing outcome data: we will analyse if the data for the studied outcome were available for all, or nearly all randomised participants; if there was any evidence that the result was biased by missing outcome data; and if the absence of the outcome was likely to depend on its true value. Bias in measurement of the outcome: we will evaluate if the method of measuring the outcome was inappropriate. We will also evaluate if the assessors of the outcome were aware of the intervention each study participant received, and if the measurement of the outcome could have differed between the experimental and control intervention groups. If applicable, we will also assess whether the assessment of the outcome was likely to have been influenced by knowledge of the intervention received. Bias in selection of the reported result: we will address whether the trial analysis was made in accordance with a predetermined plan before unblinded outcome data were available for analysis. We will also evaluate if the assessed numerical result is likely to have been selected from either multiple outcome measurements within the outcome domain or from multiple analyses of the data. If we identify any cluster‐randomised trials, we will consider an additional domain: bias arising from the timing and recruitment of participants ( Higgins 2024c ). If we identify any cross‐over trials, we will only consider the data before the cross‐over, and hence, we will assess the risk of bias as in trials with a parallel‐group design. Signalling questions in the RoB 2 tool are used to rate each domain at low risk of bias, with some concerns, or at high risk of bias ( Sterne 2019 ). Risk of bias judgements will be summarised for each outcome, across the trials that measured the outcome, for each of the domains listed. The overall risk of bias for the result will be the least favourable assessment across the domains of bias. We will use the RoB 2 Excel tool (available at www.riskofbias.info ) and store our RoB 2 data in Figshare (figshare.com). We will provide the link at the review stage. Risk of bias assessments will inform GRADE and the summary of findings tables ( Schünemann 2013 ; Schünemann 2024 ). We will assess the risk of bias for the outcomes: all‐cause mortality, proportion of participants with one or more serious adverse events, quality of life, progression‐free survival, recurrence‐free survival, proportion of participants with ORR, and proportion of participants with one or more non‐serious adverse events. In the summary of findings tables, we will also present our RoB 2 assessments of the seven outcomes. Measures of treatment effect For dichotomous variables, such as all‐cause mortality, proportion of participants with one or more serious adverse events, proportion of participants with ORR, proportion of participants with one or more non‐serious adverse events, proportion of participants with CR, proportion of participants with PR, proportion of participants with PD, and proportion of participants with SD, we will calculate risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). For continuous variables, such as quality of life, we will calculate the mean difference (MD) with 95% CIs when the outcomes are measured using the same tool across trials, or the standardised mean difference (SMD) with 95% CIs when the outcomes are measured using different tools. For time‐to‐event data, such as progression‐free survival and recurrence‐free survival, we will calculate hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% CIs. We will enter data presented as a scale with a consistent direction of effect. We will inform the reader about how to understand the scale. If data on adverse events (serious or those considered non‐serious) are reported as the number of events in each trial group, we will calculate the risk ratio from the total number of events in the separate groups of a trial with a formula in Excel ( Higgins 2024d ). We will input the data into Review Manager with an analysis set‐up of contrast level data, inverse variance method, and risk ratio (95% CI). If trial data are not reported in a format that we can enter directly into a meta‐analysis, we will convert the data to the required format, using guidance in Chapter 6 of the Cochrane Handbook ( Higgins 2024d ). We will provide all treatment groups in the characteristics of included studies table, even if they are not used in the review. Unit of analysis issues The unit of analysis will be the participants randomised to the intervention groups in the trials with a parallel‐group design. For dichotomous outcomes (e.g. presence or absence of a serious adverse event), we will use participants as units of analysis, rather than events (i.e. the number of participants with an event, rather than the number of events per participant). However, if a trial reports rate ratios, we will analyse these on the basis of events rather than participants ( Higgins 2024d ). If a trial has more than one experimental intervention group and one control intervention group that should be included in the same comparison, we will analyse data from the relevant experimental intervention groups together, if suitable to combine, and compare them with the control group. If the experimental interventions cannot be combined, but should be included in the same comparison, and they share the same control group, we will divide the participants in the control group into the number of experimental interventions ( Higgins 2024c ; Higgins 2024d ). For cluster‐randomised trials, we will analyse data by using the average cluster size and an estimate of the intracluster correlation coefficient (ICC) and the design effect to calculate the effective sample size. For cross‐over trials, we will only analyse data from the first trial period to avoid carry‐over effects ( Higgins 2024c ; Higgins 2024d ). However, we do not expect to find trials with these two types of design. If possible, we will record occasions in which multiple serious or non‐serious adverse events in a participant were incorrectly treated as independent, without taking into account the interdependence of the events. If the number of events appears to be equal to the number of participants, we will treat the events as the unit of analysis ( Higgins 2024d ). Dealing with missing data We will contact investigators or study sponsors to verify key study characteristics or obtain missing outcome data. We will calculate missing standard deviations or other necessary data using other data from the trial, such as CIs, based on methods outlined in Chapter 6 of the Cochrane Handbook , or we will impute the standard deviation from other trials in the meta‐analysis ( Furukawa 2006 ; Higgins 2024d ). We will investigate attrition rates, i.e. dropouts, losses to follow‐up, and withdrawals, and we will perform the following two sensitivity analyses of the influence of participants on incomplete or missing outcome data (risk of attrition bias) using two imputation methods, for our dichotomous outcomes ( Hollis 1999 ). Extreme‐case analysis favouring the experimental intervention ('best‐worst' case scenario): none of the dropouts/participants lost from the experimental group, but all the dropouts/participants lost from the control group will be assumed to have experienced the outcome, including all randomised participants in the denominator. Extreme‐case analysis favouring the control ('worst‐best' case scenario): all dropouts/participants lost from the experimental group, but none from the control group will be assumed to have experienced the outcome, including all randomised participants in the denominator. If we think the missing data could introduce serious bias, we will take this into consideration in the GRADE rating for the affected outcomes. We will extract the data for an ITT analysis if possible. Otherwise, we will perform a modified ITT, or available‐case analysis. We will discuss the potential impact of all missing data on our findings in the Discussion section of the review ( Page 2024 ). Assessment of heterogeneity We will assess clinical and methodological heterogeneity by describing and examining the overall characteristics of the trials, including the participants, interventions, comparisons, and trial design. Based on their diversity and similarities, we will determine if meta‐analyses are appropriate. We will look at the forest plots of trial results to consider the direction and magnitude of intervention effects and the strength of evidence for heterogeneity. We will measure statistical heterogeneity amongst the trial results in each analysis, using the I 2 statistic, and we will interpret this using the approximate guide below ( Deeks 2024 ). 0% to 40%: might not be important 30% to 60%: may represent moderate heterogeneity 50% to 90%: may represent substantial heterogeneity 75% to 100%: considerable heterogeneity If we identify substantial heterogeneity (I 2 > 50%), we will report it and explore possible causes with prespecified subgroup analyses. We will use the I² statistic to quantify inconsistencies amongst the trials in each analysis when P ≤ 0.10. We will interpret P ≤ 0.10 from the Chi² test as evidence of statistical heterogeneity ( Deeks 2024 ). We will use a random‐effects model meta‐analysis to account for the presence of between‐study heterogeneity. Assessment of reporting biases If we identify 10 or more trials with data per comparison and outcome, we will create and examine a funnel plot to analyse possible publication biases or bias of small‐study effects ( Page 2024 ). We will plot the RR on a logarithmic scale against its standard error ( Egger 1997 ). Asymmetry in a funnel plot may be observed due to small‐study effects and not just non‐reporting bias. If our searches identify any trial protocols, clinical trial registrations, or abstracts indicating the existence of unpublished trials, we will attempt to contact their authors to determine the status of these unpublished trials. We will also check trial protocols against published reports to evaluate whether selective reporting of outcomes is present. If the number of included trials per outcome is less than 10, we will not perform funnel plot analyses. Data synthesis If we judge the trials to be sufficiently similar in participants, interventions, comparators, and outcome assessment, we will conduct meta‐analyses. We will include all trials in our meta‐analyses, regardless of their risk of bias. For our primary analyses of outcome data, we will use the random‐effects meta‐analysis model with 95% CIs, as there may be variations in treatment effects. We will use the fixed‐effect model as a sensitivity analysis (secondary analysis) to the random‐effects model and ensure susceptibility to outliers ( Deeks 2024 ). If the results obtained with the two models diverge, we will present both results; otherwise, we will report only the results obtained with the random‐effects model. We will produce summary estimates of the treatment effect using Review Manager ( RevMan 2025 ). We will present data using forest plots, where possible. For time‐to‐event data, we will plot and meta‐analyse estimates of HRs and 95% CIs, as presented in the trial reports, using the generic inverse variance method in Review Manager ( RevMan 2025 ). We will not conduct meta‐analysis of outcomes reported differently (e.g. impossible to calculate the same effect measure from the available statistics) as described in Chapter 12 (Table 12.1.a) of the Cochrane Handbook . In this case, we will perform a narrative synthesis analysis ( McKenzie 2024 ). Subgroup analysis and investigation of heterogeneity We expect the following trial characteristics to introduce heterogeneity. Trials with vested interests compared to trials without vested interests: trials with vested interests may overestimate beneficial intervention effects or underestimate harmful intervention effects ( Lundh 2017 ). Trial participants with different aetiologies of HCC: because the development of HCC is attributable to different aetiologies ( Description of the condition ; McGlynn 2021 ; Singal 2020 ) Trial participants at different Child‐Pugh grades of liver function: the Child‐Pugh score is the most widely used tool to assess liver function in people with HCC and is closely related to HCC prognosis ( Description of the condition ; Duseja 2014 ; Vogel 2023 ). According to the Child‐Pugh score, people are classified into three grades: Child‐Pugh A (score 5 to 6), Child‐Pugh B (score 7 to 9), and Child‐Pugh C (score 10 to 15). Trial participants with different stages of the tumour: tumour stage is significantly associated with HCC prognosis ( Llovet 2021b ; Reig 2022 ; Vogel 2022 ). We will use a formal statistical test in Review Manager to assess subgroup differences that could account for heterogeneity, e.g. Chi² test ( RevMan 2025 ). It is recommended that at least five trials provide data for a subgroup of an outcome to ascertain if a valid subgroup difference is in effect ( Deeks 2024 ). We plan to conduct subgroup analyses for the following outcomes: all‐cause mortality, proportion of participants with one or more serious adverse events, quality of life, progression‐free survival, recurrence‐free survival, proportion of participants with ORR, and proportion of participants with one or more non‐serious adverse events. Sensitivity analysis In addition to the two sensitivity analyses described in Dealing with missing data , we also plan to perform the analyses below ( Deeks 2024 ): Excluding trials that raise some concerns or are at high risk of bias, as these may overestimate beneficial intervention effects or underestimate harmful intervention effects ( Gluud 2006 ; Guyatt 2011 ; Kjaergard 2001 ; Moher 1998 ; Savović 2012a ; Savović 2012b ; Savović 2018 ) Repeating the analysis with the fixed‐effect model Excluding trials with imputed data Trial Sequential Analysis We plan to perform Trial Sequential Analysis (TSA) on our primary outcomes only. We will perform TSA to calculate the cumulative sample size of the meta‐analysis (information size), and to reduce the risk of random errors due to sparse data and repetitive testing of accumulating data ( Castellini 2018 ; Gartlehner 2019 ; Thorlund 2017 ; TSA 2021 ; Wetterslev 2008 ). To control random errors, we will calculate the required information size (i.e. the number of participants needed in a meta‐analysis to detect or reject a certain intervention effect). The required information size calculation should also account for the diversity that is present in the meta‐analysis. We will calculate the information size adjusted for the diversity of the meta‐analysis (diversity‐adjusted required information size, DARIS) using the following parameters ( Wetterslev 2009 ). For dichotomous outcomes, we will calculate the required meta‐analysis information size based on the event proportion in the control group; assumption of a plausible relative risk reduction of 20%, or the relative risk reduction observed in the included trials at low risk of bias; with a risk of type Ⅰ error (alpha) of 2.5%; a risk of type Ⅱ error (beta) of 10%; and the observed diversity of the meta‐analysis ( Jakobsen 2014 ; Wetterslev 2009 ). For continuous outcomes, we will calculate the required information size based on the standard deviation (SD) observed in the control group of the meta‐analysis and a minimal relevant difference of 50% of this SD, and the observed diversity in the trials in the meta‐analysis. The underlying assumption of TSA is that testing for significance may be performed each time a new trial is added to the meta‐analysis. We will add the trials according to the year of publication; if more than one trial was published in a year, we will add trials alphabetically, according to the last name of the first author. On the basis of the DARIS, we will construct trial sequential monitoring boundaries ( Thorlund 2017 ; Wetterslev 2008 ; Wetterslev 2017 ). These boundaries will determine the statistical inference one may draw regarding the cumulative meta‐analysis that has not reached the DARIS. If the cumulative Z‐curve crosses the trial sequential monitoring boundary for benefit or harm before the DARIS is reached, firm evidence may be established, and further trials may be superfluous. In contrast, if the boundaries are not surpassed, it is likely necessary to continue doing trials to detect or reject a certain intervention effect. This could be determined by assessing if the cumulative Z‐curve crossed the trial sequential monitoring boundaries for futility. We will downgrade our GRADE assessments of imprecision by three, two, or one level(s), depending on how much the proportion of accrued sample size is relative to the DARIS (three levels if between 0% to 33%, two levels if between 34% to 66%, and one level if between 67% to 99%). We will not downgrade if the Z‐curve crosses the trial monitoring boundaries for benefit, harm, futility, or DARIS. A more detailed description of TSA and the software programme can be found at www.ctu.dk/tsa/ ( Thorlund 2017 ; TSA 2021 ). Summary of findings and assessment of the certainty of the evidence We will generate summary of ﬁndings tables based on the methods described in Chapter 14 of the Cochrane Handbook ( Schünemann 2024 ). We will create seven summary of ﬁndings tables, i.e. one for each of the six comparisons listed above, and another summarising all the comparisons into one table. Sorafenib versus placebo or no intervention Sorafenib with surgical resection versus surgical resection with placebo or no intervention Sorafenib with any thermal ablation technique versus the same thermal ablation technique with placebo or no intervention Sorafenib with transarterial chemoembolisation versus transarterial chemoembolisation with placebo or no intervention Sorafenib with any other drug versus the same drug (e.g. doxorubicin, capecitabine, everolimus, tigatuzumab, etc.) with placebo or no intervention Sorafenib with any other hepatocellular cancer intervention (e.g. ethanol injection) versus the same intervention (i.e. ethanol injection) with placebo or no intervention Sorafenib alone or with any hepatocellular cancer intervention versus the same cancer intervention with placebo or no intervention. We will use GRADEpro software to present the certainty of evidence for the following outcomes ( GRADEpro GDT ; Schünemann 2024 ): all‐cause mortality, proportion of participants with one or more serious adverse events, quality of life, progression‐free survival, recurrence‐free survival, proportion of participants with ORR, and proportion of participants with one or more non‐serious adverse events, at the longest follow‐up. Summary of findings tables provide information on comparative risk, risk ratio, number of participants, number of trials, and certainty of the evidence for the seven outcomes for each review comparison. We will use the five GRADE domains: overall risk of bias, consistency of effect, indirectness, imprecision (using a minimally contextualised approach ( Zeng 2022 )), and publication bias, to assess the certainty of a body of evidence ensuing from the trials with meta‐analysed data of specified outcomes. If a meta‐analysis is not possible, we will still present the outcome and enter relevant information in the comments field of the tables. For the risk of bias, we will use the overall judgement for the outcome. Low risk of bias indicates no limitation (the certainty is not downgraded). Some concerns indicate either no limitation or serious limitation (the certainty is downgraded one level). High risk of bias indicates either serious limitation or very serious limitation (the certainty is downgraded two levels). We will justify all decisions to downgrade the certainty of the evidence using footnotes, and make comments to aid the reader's understanding of the review, where necessary. The levels of evidence are defined as follows: High certainty: we are very confident that the true effect lies close to that of the estimate of the effect. Moderate certainty: we are moderately confident in the effect estimate; the true effect is likely to be close to the estimate of the effect, but there is a possibility that it is substantially different. Low certainty: our confidence in the effect estimate is limited; the true effect may be substantially different from the estimate of the effect. Very low certainty: we have very little confidence in the effect estimate; the true effect is likely to be substantially different from the estimate of effect. Two review authors (SC and SD) will independently make judgements, with disagreements resolved by discussion. If disagreements are not resolved, a third review author (WL) will arbitrate. We will justify, document, and incorporate judgments into the reporting of results for each outcome. During the work on our review, we will follow this protocol, and we will report any deviations from it in the Differences between protocol and review section of the finished review. documents.title: Combined pharmacological and psychosocial interventions for alcohol use disorder.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a mental disorder characterised by a strong desire to consume alcohol and impaired control of alcohol use, with devastating consequences. Many people with AUD do not respond to psychosocial or pharmacological interventions when these are provided alone. Combining these interventions may improve the response to treatment, though evidence remains limited.
OBJECTIVES: To assess the effects of combined pharmacological and psychosocial interventions for the treatment of AUD in adults.
SEARCH METHODS: We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, three other databases, and two trials registers in November 2023, without language restrictions.
SELECTION CRITERIA: We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing combined pharmacological and psychosocial interventions versus pharmacological or psychosocial interventions alone, or no intervention/treatment as usual (TAU), in adults with AUD. Our primary outcomes were continuous abstinent participants, frequency of use (measured as heavy drinkers, percentages of abstinent days, heavy-drinking days), amount of use (number of drinks per drinking day), adverse events, serious adverse events, dropouts from treatment, and dropouts due to adverse events.
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: We assessed risk of bias using Cochrane's RoB 1 tool, performed random-effects meta-analyses, and evaluated the certainty of evidence according to the GRADE approach.
MAIN RESULTS: We included 21 RCTs (4746 participants). The most studied pharmacological and psychosocial interventions were naltrexone (81.0%) and cognitive behavioural therapy (66.7%), respectively. Most participants were men (74%), aged about 44 years, with AUD, without comorbid mental disorders or other substance use disorders; 15 RCTs detoxified participants before treatment. We judged 28.5% of the studies as at low risk of bias for random sequence generation, allocation concealment, performance bias for objective and subjective outcomes, and detection bias for subjective outcomes; all studies were at low risk of detection bias for objective outcomes; 85.7% of studies were at low risk of attrition bias; 14.2% of studies were at low risk of reporting bias. 1) Compared to psychosocial intervention alone, combined pharmacological and psychosocial interventions probably reduce the number of heavy drinkers (above the clinically meaningful threshold (MID) of 2%; absolute difference (AD) -10%, 95% confidence interval (CI) -18% to -2%; risk ratio (RR) 0.86, 95% CI 0.76 to 0.97; 8 studies, 1609 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). They may increase continuous abstinent participants (MID 5%; AD 5%, 95% CI 1% to 11%; RR 1.17, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.34; 6 studies, 1184 participants; low-certainty evidence). They probably have little to no effect on: • the rate of abstinent days (MID 8%; mean difference (MD) 4.16, 95% CI 1.24 to 7.08; 10 studies, 2227 participants); • serious adverse events (MID 1%; AD -2%, 95% CI -3% to 0%; RR 0.20, 95% CI 0.03 to 1.12; 4 studies; 524 participants); • dropouts from treatment (MID 10%; AD -3%, 95% CI -5% to 0%; RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.01; 15 studies, 3021 participants); and • dropouts due to adverse events (MID 5%; AD 2%, 95% CI 0% to 5%; RR 1.91, 95% CI 1.04 to 3.52; 8 studies, 1572 participants) (all moderate-certainty evidence). They may have little to no effect on: • heavy-drinking days (MID 5%; MD -3.49, 95% CI -8.68 to 1.70; 4 studies, 470 participants); • number of drinks per drinking day (MID 1 drink; MD -0.57, 95% CI -1.16 to 0.01; 7 studies, 805 participants); and • adverse events (MID 30%; AD 17%, 95% CI -5% to 46%; RR 1.25, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.68; 4 studies, 508 participants) (all low-certainty evidence). 2) Compared to pharmacological intervention alone, combined pharmacological and psychosocial interventions may have little to no effect on: • the rate of abstinent days (MID 8%; MD -1.18, 95% CI -4.42 to 2.07; 2 studies, 1158 participants); and • dropouts from treatment (MID 10%; AD 1%, 95% CI -10 to 14%; RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.47; 3 studies, 1246 participants) (all low-certainty evidence). We are uncertain about their effect on: • continuous abstinent participants (MID 5%; AD 3%, 95% CI -5% to 18%; RR 1.22, 95% CI 0.62 to 2.40; 1 study, 241 participants); • the number of heavy drinkers (MID 2%; AD 2%, 95% CI -4% to 8%; RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.12; 1 study, 917 participants); • the number of drinks per drinking day (MID 1 drink; MD -2.40, 95% CI -3.98 to -0.82; 1 study, 241 participants); and • dropouts due to adverse events (MID 5%; AD -1%, 95% CI -3% to 6%; RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.14 to 2.72; 2 studies, 1165 participants) (all very low-certainty evidence). 3) We are uncertain about the effect of combined pharmacological and psychosocial interventions, when compared to TAU, on: • the number of heavy drinkers (MID 2%; AD -5%, 95% CI -13% to 2%; RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.03; 1 study, 616 participants); • the rate of abstinent days (MID 8%; MD 3.43, 95% CI -1.32 to 8.18; 1 study, 616 participants); • dropouts from treatment (MID 10%; AD 0%, 95% CI -10% to 15%; RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.65; 2 studies, 696 participants); and • dropouts due to adverse events (MID 5%; AD 3%, 95% CI 0% to 15%; RR 2.97, 95% CI 0.70 to 12.67; 1 study, 616 participants) (all very low-certainty evidence). The certainty of evidence ranged from moderate to very low, downgraded mainly due to risk of bias and imprecision.
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: As implications for practice, our findings indicate that adding pharmacological to psychosocial interventions is safe and helps people with AUD recover. These conclusions are based on low- to moderate-certainty evidence. Given the few studies and very low-certainty evidence, any benefits of adding psychosocial to pharmacological interventions or comparing the combined intervention to TAU are less clear. As implications for research, further studies should investigate the effects of the combined intervention compared to pharmacotherapy or TAU.

documents.title: Corticosteroids for treating sepsis in children and adults.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sepsis occurs when an infection is complicated by organ failure. Sepsis may be complicated by impaired corticosteroid metabolism. Thus, providing corticosteroids may benefit patients. This is an update of a review originally published in 2004 and previously updated in 2010, 2015 and 2019.
OBJECTIVES: To examine the benefits and harms of corticosteroids in children and adults with sepsis.
SEARCH METHODS: We searched CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, ClinicalTrials.gov, ISRCTN and the WHO Clinical Trials Search Portal on 31 December 2023. In addition, we conducted reference checking and citation research, and contacted study authors, to identify additional studies as needed. We updated this search in December 2024, but these results have not yet been incorporated.
SELECTION CRITERIA: We included randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of corticosteroids versus placebo or usual care (antimicrobials, fluid replacement and vasopressor therapy as needed) in children and adults with sepsis. We also included RCTs of continuous infusion versus intermittent bolus of corticosteroids.
DATA COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS: We used the same methods in comparisons of corticosteroids versus placebo or usual care, and of continuous infusion versus intermittent bolus administration of corticosteroids. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality at 28 days. The most critical secondary outcomes were (i) all-cause mortality in the long term (last follow-up from 90 days to one year) and in the hospital; (ii) length of stay in the intensive care unit and in hospital; (iii) adverse effects, i.e. superinfection and muscle weakness (within 28 days). All review authors screened and selected studies for inclusion. One review author extracted data, which was checked by the others, and by the lead author of the primary study when possible. For this update, we used Covidence software for screening and selection of studies and abstraction of data by paired review authors, with discrepancies resolved by a third review author. We obtained unpublished data from the authors of some trials. We assessed the risk of bias in trials using the Cochrane risk of bias tool (RoB 1) and applied GRADE to assess the certainty of evidence. The review authors did not contribute to the assessment of eligibility or risk of bias, nor to data extraction, for the trials they had participated in.
MAIN RESULTS: We included 87 trials (24,336 participants), of which six included only children, two included children and adults, and the remaining trials included only adults. Seventeen additional trials are ongoing and will be considered in future versions of this review. We judged 25 trials as being at low risk of bias. Corticosteroids versus placebo or usual care Compared to placebo or usual care, corticosteroids probably reduce 28-day mortality (risk ratio (RR) 0.89, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.84 to 0.95; 72 trials, 22,915 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). We downgraded the certainty of evidence for this outcome from high to moderate for inconsistency (significant heterogeneity across trial results). Corticosteroids may result in little to no difference in long-term mortality (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.03; 12 trials, 8468 participants; low-certainty evidence) and probably reduce in-hospital mortality (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.84 to 0.97; 40 trials, 17,459 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Corticosteroids may reduce length of intensive care unit (ICU) stay for all participants (mean difference (MD) -0.86 days, 95% CI -1.67 to -0.05; 25 trials, 8069 participants; low-certainty evidence) and may reduce length of hospital stay for all participants (MD -1.09 days, 95% CI -1.85 to -0.34; 31 trials, 16,954 participants; low-certainty evidence). The evidence is uncertain about the effect of corticosteroids on the risk of muscle weakness (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.53; 7 trials, 6729 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Corticosteroids may result in little to no difference in the risk of superinfection (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.07; 36 trials, 7961 participants; low-certainty evidence). Continuous infusion of corticosteroids versus intermittent bolus Four trials reported data for this comparison, and the certainty of evidence for all outcomes was very low. We are uncertain about the effects of continuous infusion of corticosteroids compared with intermittent bolus administration on 28-day mortality (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.32; 3 trials, 310 participants). We downgraded the certainty of evidence to very low due to high risk of bias in all except one trial and due to imprecision. Compared to bolus administration, we are uncertain of the effects of continuous infusion of corticosteroids on long-term mortality (RR 1.36, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.81; 1 trial, 70 participants; very low-certainty evidence), in-hospital mortality (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.19; 3 trials, 352 participants; very low-certainty evidence), ICU length of stay amongst all participants (MD -0.56 days, 95% CI -3.44 to 2.32; 4 trials, 422 participants; very low-certainty evidence), hospital length of stay amongst all participants (MD -0.21 days, 95% CI -4.72 to 4.30; 4 trials, 422 participants; very low-certainty evidence), risk of muscle weakness (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.13 to 5.98; 1 trial, 70 participants; very low-certainty evidence) and risk of superinfection (RR 1.12, 95% CI 0.37 to 3.33; 2 trials, 193 participants; very low-certainty evidence).
AUTHORS' CONCLUSIONS: Moderate-certainty evidence indicates that corticosteroids probably reduce 28-day, 90-day and hospital mortality amongst patients with sepsis. Corticosteroids may shorten ICU and hospital length of stay (low-certainty evidence). There may be little or no difference in the risk of superinfection. The risk of muscle weakness is uncertain. The effects of continuous versus intermittent bolus administration of corticosteroids are uncertain.

documents.title: Prevalence, incidence, systemic, behavioral, and patient-related risk factors and indicators for peri-implant diseases: An AO/AAP  systematic review and meta-analysis.
documents.abstract:
BACKGROUND: A profound understanding of the epidemiology of peri-implant diseases (PIDs) is essential for the development of preventive approaches to mitigate the occurrence and progression of peri-implant biological complications. The present systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to assess the incidence, prevalence, systemic, behavioral, and patient-related risk indicators and factors for PIDs in adult patients with dental implants.
METHODS: Clinical studies assessing the prevalence, incidence, systemic risk indicators, and risk factors for PIDs were considered eligible for inclusion. MEDLINE-PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Central Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov electronic databases were searched for published articles. Pooled data analyses were performed using random-effects models to identify risk indicators and factors for PIDs.
RESULTS: Of 1120 potentially eligible records, 102 studies met the eligibility criteria and were included in this systematic review. Prevalence rates at the patient level for peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis were 46% (95% confidence interval [CI], 41-51) and 21% (95% CI, 17-24), respectively. Weighted mean incidence rates at the patient level for peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis were 53% and 22%, respectively, within 20 years of function. Pooled estimates identified periodontitis, obesity, and smoking habits as significant systemic risk indicators for mucositis. For peri-implantitis, the significant risk indicators were periodontitis, diabetes mellitus, smoking habits, and alcohol consumption. Only risk indicators could be identified in the selected evidence.
CONCLUSION: More than half of the patients treated with dental implants were affected by PIDs over a 10-year follow-up period, with peri-implant mucositis being the most prevalent condition. Periodontitis and smoking were identified as risk indicators for the development of both PIDs. Obesity was identified as a potential risk indicator for mucositis, while diabetes mellitus and alcohol consumption were recognized as potential risk indicators for peri-implantitis.
PLAIN LANGUAGE SUMMARY: This systematic review looked at the causes and frequency of problems around dental implants, known as PIDs, which include conditions like peri-implant mucositis (inflammation around the implant) and peri-implantitis (more serious infection around the implant). Understanding these conditions and their etiology is important for finding ways to prevent them. This research reviewed 102 studies (including 13,030 patients) to gather data on how often these problems occur and what factors might increase the risk of developing them. The meta-analyses revealed that nearly half of people with dental implants had peri-implant mucositis, and about one in five had peri-implantitis. Over a period of 20 years, the incidence rates for developing these conditions were about 53% for mucositis and 22% for peri-implantitis. The study identified certain health and lifestyle factors that could increase the risk of these conditions. For mucositis, risk factors included having gum disease (periodontitis), obesity, and smoking. For peri-implantitis, the risks were similar, with periodontitis, smoking, and diabetes and alcohol use being important factors.

Abstract Background A profound understanding of the epidemiology of peri‐implant diseases (PIDs) is essential for the development of preventive approaches to mitigate the occurrence and progression of peri‐implant biological complications. The present systematic review and meta‐analysis aimed to assess the incidence, prevalence, systemic, behavioral, and patient‐related risk indicators and factors for PIDs in adult patients with dental implants. Methods Clinical studies assessing the prevalence, incidence, systemic risk indicators, and risk factors for PIDs were considered eligible for inclusion. MEDLINE–PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Central Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov electronic databases were searched for published articles. Pooled data analyses were performed using random‐effects models to identify risk indicators and factors for PIDs. Results Of 1120 potentially eligible records, 102 studies met the eligibility criteria and were included in this systematic review. Prevalence rates at the patient level for peri‐implant mucositis and peri‐implantitis were 46% (95% confidence interval [CI], 41–51) and 21% (95% CI, 17–24), respectively. Weighted mean incidence rates at the patient level for peri‐implant mucositis and peri‐implantitis were 53% and 22%, respectively, within 20 years of function. Pooled estimates identified periodontitis, obesity, and smoking habits as significant systemic risk indicators for mucositis. For peri‐implantitis, the significant risk indicators were periodontitis, diabetes mellitus, smoking habits, and alcohol consumption. Only risk indicators could be identified in the selected evidence. Conclusion More than half of the patients treated with dental implants were affected by PIDs over a 10‐year follow‐up period, with peri‐implant mucositis being the most prevalent condition. Periodontitis and smoking were identified as risk indicators for the development of both PIDs. Obesity was identified as a potential risk indicator for mucositis, while diabetes mellitus and alcohol consumption were recognized as potential risk indicators for peri‐implantitis. Plain Language Summary This systematic review looked at the causes and frequency of problems around dental implants, known as PIDs, which include conditions like peri‐implant mucositis (inflammation around the implant) and peri‐implantitis (more serious infection around the implant). Understanding these conditions and their etiology is important for finding ways to prevent them. This research reviewed 102 studies (including 13,030 patients) to gather data on how often these problems occur and what factors might increase the risk of developing them. The meta‐analyses revealed that nearly half of people with dental implants had peri‐implant mucositis, and about one in five had peri‐implantitis. Over a period of 20 years, the incidence rates for developing these conditions were about 53% for mucositis and 22% for peri‐implantitis. The study identified certain health and lifestyle factors that could increase the risk of these conditions. For mucositis, risk factors included having gum disease (periodontitis), obesity, and smoking.
